title: Promissory Offices: Succession Rules Replace Diachronic Identity
thesis: When a promisor's later stage is not psychologically continuous with the stage that promised, the promise binds that later stage only if the promise was made from within an office: a normatively individuated position with publicly specifiable succession rules. Personal identity matters in ordinary promising only because it is the default succession rule for the office of 'being this person'.
argument_sketch: Corporate promises survive complete staff turnover, and no one thinks a corporation's memory is what grounds this. They survive because the corporation's charter, together with legal and conventional rules, fixes which later agents occupy the promising position. I generalize this. Every promise is issued from a position, and its normative reach is set by that position's succession conditions. For natural persons the default succession rule is psychological continuity, which explains why identity looks essential. The default is not mandatory, however: AI deployments and dementia care can set up alternative succession rules, such as designated successors, standing instructions, or role-holders. Where no succession rule picks out the later stage, the promise lapses. The view therefore yields determinate verdicts in all three cases and explains why each one feels different.
why_new: Theories of corporate moral agency (French, List and Pettit) treat corporations as persons with their own identity conditions. Personal-identity ethics (Parfit, Schechtman) treats the individual case separately. This thesis reverses the direction of explanation and makes office-succession the general schema, with personal identity as one instance. It also supplies a criterion, 'is there a succession rule picking out this stage?', which current literature on normative powers (Raz, Owens, Chang) lacks.

objection.objection: The office analogy hides the real source of the successor's obligation, and once that source is exposed the view either fails to deliver promissory bindingness or assumes the authority it claims to explain. Office-holders who inherit a predecessor's commitments are bound because they occupy the office under rules whose normative force comes from somewhere: either their own acceptance of the office (taking the job, swearing the oath, accepting the trust) or a legitimate authority entitled to impose duties on them (the legal order that issues the charter). Neither source is the original promise. In the corporate case the promisor never changes. The corporation is the obligor, and it persists across staff turnover through its decision procedures (List & Pettit, Group Agency, 2011). Staff carry role-duties to discharge the corporation's obligations under employment terms they agreed to. So the case does not show that a promise binds a later, distinct agent through a succession rule. It shows that a persisting group agent's promise is carried out by role-holders who are bound for independent reasons. Generalizing to natural persons then breaks down. Nobody enacts the 'default succession rule' of psychological continuity, and nothing in the account explains its authority. In the cases the thesis is designed for (the person with severe dementia, the redeployed AI), the later stage has not accepted any office, and no one has been shown to hold the normative power to impose one. If the earlier stage sets the succession rule itself, it is binding a non-continuous agent without that agent's consent. That runs into the ordinary principle that I cannot promise on another's behalf without authority to do so (cf. Hart 1955 and Raz 1972 on normative powers, Owens 2012 on promissory interests). Whether the earlier stage has that authority is exactly the question at issue. If carers, deployers, or the law set the rule instead, the resulting duties are imposed role-obligations, and the thesis has changed the subject from promising to stipulated responsibility.
objection.rationale: This attacks the paper's central inference (corporate case → all promises are issued from offices) and its main explanatory claim (identity is just the default succession rule), not a detail. If it stands unanswered, the corporate case no longer supports the view, because a persisting obligor plus role-duties grounded in consent explains it equally well or better. The 'determinate verdicts' in the dementia and AI cases also become question-begging, because they depend on a power to bind a non-identical successor that the paper never justifies. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because a response is available, though it is costly. The author could argue that offices can carry obligations without the incumbent's consent, as with inherited debts against an estate or a minor's guardianship duties, and that promissory obligation is fundamentally positional rather than agent-relative, perhaps along Scanlon's Principle F lines with the expectation-holder's claim attaching to the position. Even so, the author would need to (a) show that such cases are promissory and not merely compensatory or role-based, and (b) give an account of who holds the power to set succession rules for natural persons that does not quietly bring back psychological continuity or consent. Without that, the thesis turns into a theory of role-obligation that merely shares a name with promising.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency: An Essay in Revisionary Metaphysics (Princeton UP, 1998)
closest_work.relation: This is the closest precedent for the core move. Rovane argues that the condition of personal identity is normative and agential rather than psychological-continuity-based. She holds that persons are individuated by a commitment to achieving rational unity, so that group persons and multiple persons within one human are possible. Your claim that 'being this person' is a normatively individuated position that psychological continuity merely fills by default is a close cousin. The main differences are that you foreground succession rules and promissory reach. Rovane foregrounds the rational point of view and does not use an office-and-succession apparatus.

closest_work.work: Christian List & Philip Pettit, Group Agency (OUP, 2011), esp. ch. 8 'Personifying Group Agents'; cf. Pettit's performative conception of the person
closest_work.relation: This work supplies your corporate premise and much of your generalization. List and Pettit explain how group agents persist through total membership turnover via organizational structure. They also defend a performative conception: to be a person is to be able to make and be held to commitments in a space of mutual address. Your view adds explicit succession rules and makes individual personal identity a default instance of that performative office. But the inference from the corporate case to a conventional, role-based account of personhood is already present in this framework.

closest_work.work: Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan ch. 16 ('Of Persons, Authors, and Things Personated'); F. W. Maitland, 'The Corporation Sole' (LQR 1900); Ernst Kantorowicz, The King's Two Bodies (1957)
closest_work.relation: This is the historical source of the 'office' model. Hobbes treats 'person' as a persona or role and distinguishes natural from artificial persons. Maitland and Kantorowicz analyze offices such as the Crown and the parson whose obligations pass to successors under fixed succession rules ('the king never dies'). Your thesis effectively proposes that every natural person is a corporation sole whose default succession rule is psychological continuity. That inversion is the genuinely interesting part, but the conceptual machinery is old. Locke's description of 'person' as 'a forensic term' (Essay II.xxvii.26) is also in the background.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (OUP, 1984), Part III, esp. the club/nation analogy and the nineteenth-century Russian nobleman case (ch. 15)
closest_work.relation: Parfit already argues that personal identity is like the identity of a club, often a matter of convention or decision, and that it is not what matters. He explicitly tests this against commitments and promises across weakened connectedness. The Russian case is about whether an earlier self's commitment binds a later, discontinuous self, and whether a third party, the wife, may act as its custodian. Your 'designated successor' idea answers Parfit's own puzzle. You need to engage this case directly.

closest_work.work: Marya Schechtman, Staying Alive: Personal Identity, Practical Concerns, and the Unity of a Life (OUP, 2014); Hilde Lindemann, Holding and Letting Go (OUP, 2014)
closest_work.relation: Schechtman's Person Life View individuates persons partly by their place in a socially structured form of life and addresses dementia explicitly. Lindemann argues that others 'hold' a person in identity through social practices, again with dementia as the central case. Both already detach person-continuity from strict psychological continuity in the dementia case by appealing to socially constituted roles. That partly pre-empts your claim that dementia care can install alternative succession rules.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993) on precedent autonomy; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia: Elegant Theory, Questionable Policy', Hastings Center Report 25(6) (1995)
closest_work.relation: This is the established debate over whether an earlier competent self's commitments, such as advance directives, bind a later demented stage. Dresser presses discontinuity objections. Your dementia verdicts must be positioned against this literature. As it stands, your thesis does not say whether a standing instruction binds the later stage or authorizes third parties to act on it, which is exactly where Dworkin and Dresser disagree.

closest_work.work: Peter French, 'The Corporation as a Moral Person' (APQ 1979) and Collective and Corporate Responsibility (1984)
closest_work.relation: This is the classic source for the corporate-internal-decision-structure account of corporate agency. It already argues that a corporation's charter and decision procedures, not any shared memory, individuate the responsible corporate agent over time.

novelty.note:
I have not seen the specific packaging published: promissory bindingness across psychological discontinuity is fixed by the succession rules of the position promised from, with personal identity as merely the default succession rule, applied uniformly to corporations, AI deployments, and dementia. But each component is well established. The normative and agential individuation of persons comes from Rovane and Korsgaard ('Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency', PPA 1989). The performative or role conception of personhood and group persistence through turnover come from List and Pettit and from French. The office-with-succession model comes from Hobbes, Maitland, and Kantorowicz. Identity as conventional and not what matters, tested on promises, comes from Parfit. Social maintenance of identity in dementia comes from Schechtman and Lindemann. So the novelty claim must rest on the unification and the determinate verdicts, and those are where the argument is weakest.

The first problem is that the corporate analogy cuts against you. On List and Pettit's account, the corporation remains the same agent across turnover. The promise binds the corporation, not the later staff members as such. So the case supports 'the promisor's identity conditions can be non-psychological'. It does not support 'promises can bind a non-identical later stage via succession rules'. You need to say which of these is your thesis. The first is Rovane's. The second is new but unsupported by your lead example.

The second problem is that 'designated successor' looks like assignment or novation, not binding a later stage. When a dementia patient's proxy or an AI deployment's role-holder inherits the obligation, the natural description is that a different agent has taken on, or been assigned, a duty. Contract law already handles that through assignment, delegation, and novation, which typically require the promisee's consent for duties. You should explain why the promisee's consent is not required for re-routing the obligation, or concede that it is. Conceding it undercuts the claim that succession rules alone fix promissory reach.

The third problem is the authority regress. Who fixes the succession rules for the office of 'being this person', and by what standing? For corporations the answer is charter plus law. For natural persons, if the answer is 'convention', you need an account of how the promisor can unilaterally alter it. The AI and dementia cases require such alteration. Otherwise any promisor could launder obligations by pre-designating a successor. If the answer is that the promisor can alter it, you owe a constraint on opportunistic succession rules. If the answer is that no one can alter it, the default is mandatory after all.

The fourth problem is that the 'lapse' verdict is underspecified. Saying the promise lapses where no rule picks out the later stage presupposes that some rule determinately applies or fails to apply. Parfit's point was that in hard cases there is no fact about continuity. Your view inherits that indeterminacy unless succession rules are sharper than continuity, and in dementia they are not.

The fifth problem is the explanatory claim. That 'each case feels different' is offered as explanatory payoff without any independent account of the phenomenology. Either drop it or argue for it.

Recommendation: reframe the paper as a contribution to the Rovane and List–Pettit line, engage Parfit's Russian nobleman and the Dworkin–Dresser debate directly, and distinguish binding the later stage from transferring the obligation.

title: Procurement Promises and the Retroactive Location of Breach
thesis: A promise made by an agent that knows its future stage will be discontinuous imposes an obligation only on the promising stage: an obligation to make it the case now that the promised performance will occur. When the later stage fails to perform, the wrong is attributed retroactively to the promising stage's inadequate procurement, not to the later stage.
argument_sketch: Ordinary 'result promises' already exist, as in 'I promise the package will arrive', and their content concerns outcomes rather than the promisor's own later conduct. When continuity is unavailable, a sincere promisor can intend only to set up the conditions for performance, so the promise's content changes from self-performance to procurement. Breach can then be a past-tense fact made true by later events. This is a familiar structure from cases like negligently building a bridge that collapses years later. The view explains why we resent the AI developer, the corporation's former board, or the pre-dementia self rather than the hapless later stage. It also yields a distinctive duty of disclosure: a promisor who cannot procure must say so.
why_new: Existing accounts assume the wrong of breach occurs at the time of non-performance (Scanlon's Principle F, Owens's authority view). This thesis argues that for discontinuous promisors the locus of breach is the promising act, while its truth-maker is later. That separates the time of wronging from the time of its grounds in a way the promising literature has not explored, and it gives a principled account of who is blameworthy in each of the three cases.

objection.objection: The argument's central mechanism, a breach by the promising stage that later non-performance makes true retroactively, fails because 'inadequate procurement' cannot be defined both independently of the outcome and dependently on it. Suppose adequacy is fixed by what the promising stage did: its diligence, the safeguards it built, its reasonable expectations. Then whether the later stage performs is irrelevant to whether the earlier stage did wrong. A promisor who procured flawlessly did no wrong when performance later fails, and a negligent one did wrong even if performance happens by luck. On that reading, nothing is made true 'retroactively'. Suppose instead adequacy is fixed by the outcome, so that procurement counts as inadequate just because performance did not occur. Then 'inadequate procurement' is a relabelled strict guarantee. That raises two problems. First, a sincere promisor cannot intend to discharge such a guarantee: when the later stage is a discontinuous free agent, such as a new board, a retrained model, or a later self with different values, nothing done now can make it the case that the later stage will act. Ought-implies-can then makes the promise void or insincere, which is exactly what the 'sincere promisor can intend only to procure' premise was meant to avoid. Second, the diagnostic payoff disappears. We do not and should not resent a developer or former board that took every reasonable precaution, yet strict liability makes them wrongdoers anyway. The bridge analogy does not help on either reading. In negligent construction the moral wrong is complete when the bridge is built. The later collapse adds harm and legal liability, not wrongness, unless one embraces resultant moral luck (Williams 1976; Nagel 1979), which then needs to be argued for rather than borrowed. Ordinary result promises ('the package will arrive') also do not help. As Thomson (The Realm of Rights, 1990, ch. 12) notes, they work as warranties: the promisor owes compensation on failure but has not wronged anyone by a faulty act. They are not obligations to have done enough, discovered after the fact.
objection.rationale: The objection targets the core of the thesis, namely the retroactive-breach structure and the claim that our resentment tracks 'inadequate procurement'. It is not aimed at an incidental premise. Each way out costs the view something essential. Taking the fault reading makes the thesis an ordinary negligence-at-time-of-promising view. That view is plausible but not new, and it needs no retroactivity, no bridge analogy and no change of content. It also leaves unexplained why the later stage's free refusal is no one's breach. Taking the strict reading makes the view a warranty view. That view cannot support sincere intention, misdescribes the promisor's fault, and collides with successor liability: corporate law in fact binds the current entity, not the former board. That collision undermines the corporate case offered as support. The disclosure duty survives on either reading, which is why I rate this 4 and not 5. That duty is a genuine and defensible result, but it follows from Scanlon's Principle F (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998, ch. 7) without the rest of the apparatus. The author might reply with a mixed view: fault-based wrongness, with blameworthiness amplified by the outcome. But that reply has to be built and defended explicitly, and it moves the paper's centre of gravity into the moral-luck literature.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), esp. §§ on the Russian nobleman and on commitments across psychological discontinuity (Part III, ch. 15)
closest_work.relation: The central precedent. Parfit asks whether commitments made by an earlier self bind a later, psychologically discontinuous self. He suggests the earlier self may lack authority over the later one. Your thesis is a specific resolution of Parfit's puzzle: shift the obligation's content and bearer to the earlier stage. The problem space is therefore not new. The 'procurement' resolution is the distinctive move.

closest_work.work: T. M. Scanlon, 'Promises and Practices' (Phil & Public Affairs 1990) and What We Owe to Each Other (1998), ch. 7: Principles D (due care), L (loss prevention), EF and F (fidelity)
closest_work.relation: Your 'distinctive duty of disclosure' is essentially Scanlon's Principle D, plus the duty to warn in Principle L: do not lead others to form expectations you have reason to believe will be disappointed, and warn them when you know you won't perform. It is not distinctive to your view. Scanlon also makes it independent of the promise's content, which undercuts your claim that the procurement analysis 'yields' it.

closest_work.work: Civil-law distinction between obligation de résultat and obligation de moyens (René Demogue, Traité des obligations, 1925); English contract-law 'procure' covenants ('X shall procure that Y does Z'); guarantees and warranties; O. W. Holmes, 'The Path of the Law' (1897)
closest_work.relation: The 'result promise' and 'procurement' contents you rely on are long-established doctrinal categories. Law has already worked out promises to bring about others' performance, including liability when the third party defaults. Your argument needs to engage this, because the law's answer is usually strict liability for the result. It is not liability for 'inadequate procurement', which you conflate (see note).

closest_work.work: Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'The Time of a Killing' (J Phil 1971); George Pitcher, 'The Misfortunes of the Dead' (APQ 1984); Thomas Nagel and Bernard Williams, 'Moral Luck' (1976/1979)
closest_work.relation: These cover the structure of a wrong whose occurrence is made true by later events, which you illustrate with the bridge case. Thomson addresses when an act becomes a killing. Pitcher defends antemortem persons harmed in virtue of postmortem events. Nagel's negligent driver is your bridge case. This component is well-trodden and should be cited rather than presented as an independent discovery.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993) on precedent autonomy; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia' (Hastings Center Report 1995); Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (2002) on time-relative interests
closest_work.relation: The dementia application has an extensive literature on the earlier self's authority over the later self, including advance directives as 'Ulysses contracts'. Note the direction. That debate is mostly about whether the earlier self's directives bind or override the later self. Yours is about relocating the obligation backward. The data point that 'we resent the pre-dementia self' is not obviously true and is not supported by that literature.

closest_work.work: Michael Bratman, 'Time, Rationality, and Self-Governance' (2012) and planning-agency work; Edward Hinchman, 'Trust and Diachronic Agency' (Noûs 2003)
closest_work.relation: These works ground diachronic commitment in cross-temporal self-trust and planning structure. They are relevant to your claim that without continuity a sincere promisor 'can intend only' to set up conditions. Bratman's account of intentions that settle future conduct via non-self-continuous mechanisms is the natural place to test that claim.

closest_work.work: Andreas Matthias, 'The Responsibility Gap' (Ethics & IT 2004); Robert Sparrow, 'Killer Robots' (J Applied Phil 2007)
closest_work.relation: The AI-developer case falls under responsibility-gap debates, which already discuss tracing responsibility back to designers. Your view is a promissory variant of the 'trace back to the designer' response that Sparrow considers and rejects.

novelty.note:
Every component is established: Parfitian discontinuous commitment, result/procurement promises, retroactively-completed wrongs, the duty to disclose non-performance, and back-tracing responsibility to designers/boards/earlier selves. I know of no published work that combines them into exactly this thesis: a known-discontinuity promise has its content shifted to present procurement, with breach retroactively located in the promising stage. But I cannot rule out recent work on promising by LLM-based agents. Search 2023-26 venues (e.g., Philosophy & Technology, Minds and Machines) for 'AI promising'/'chatbot commitments' before claiming novelty. So: 'partly'. The synthesis may be new; the parts are not, and the paper currently presents several of them as though they were.

Substantive problems a referee would press:
(1) The core tension: means vs. result. You say the obligation is 'to make it the case now that performance will occur' (a result obligation) and also that breach consists in 'inadequate procurement' (a means/diligence obligation). These come apart. If the stage procured with full diligence and the later stage still defaulted, the result view says breach and the diligence view says none. If the obligation is result-type, the wrong does not lie in any inadequacy of procurement. It is strict liability, and the 'retroactive attribution to inadequate procurement' story is false. If it is diligence-type, non-performance is not breach at all, so nothing is made true retroactively. You must pick one. Each option loses a selling point.
(2) The content-shift argument is a non sequitur. From 'a sincere promisor can only intend to procure', it does not follow that the promise's content becomes procurement. It may instead follow that the promise is insincere or defective, or that it was a guarantee all along. Sincerity constrains what one may promise, not what one's words mean. Engage the 'promising beyond one's control' literature (e.g., debates over whether 'I promise it'll arrive' is a genuine promise or a guarantee/assurance).
(3) The AI and corporation cases change the agent. In the dementia case one organism promises. In the AI case the developer typically made no promise; the AI (stage) did. Blaming the developer is then not attributing the promise's breach to 'the promising stage'. It is third-party negligence, which needs no promissory theory. The corporate case depends on whether the board or the corporation promised (List & Pettit, Group Agency, 2011). As stated, the 'explanatory payoff' trades on equivocation over who the promisor is.
(4) The resentment data are contested. Many people do direct resentment at the defaulting corporation now, not its former board, and successor liability in law tracks that. The dementia case is precisely where intuitions split (Dresser vs. Dworkin). The phenomenology cannot do the evidential work you assign it.
(5) The stage metaphysics is unaddressed. If you are a stage theorist (Sider, Four-Dimensionalism, 2001), all promises are made by stages and all would be procurement promises, which over-generalizes. If you are not, you owe an account of which discontinuities trigger the content shift and why the trigger is the promisor's knowledge of discontinuity rather than the discontinuity itself.

title: Assumption by Self-Ascription
thesis: A psychologically discontinuous later stage becomes bound by an earlier stage's promise when, and because, it ascribes that promise to itself in the first person ('I promised you X') in interaction with the promisee. First-person self-ascription of a commitment is itself a normative act of assumption, not a mere report.
argument_sketch: A conversational AI instance reading a transcript says 'as I told you earlier, I'll do X'. A corporation's new spokesperson says 'we committed to this'. In both cases the speaker could have disowned the commitment and instead claimed it. Following Austin and Searle on performatives, I argue that in contexts where ownership is genuinely open, the self-ascription has a constitutive force similar to accepting an assignment of a debt. The promisee may rely on the self-ascription, and the speaker is estopped from disclaiming it, because self-ascription draws on the trust the original promise generated. The thesis predicts that a later stage that never self-ascribes, such as a severely demented patient, is not bound, while an AI instance that does self-ascribe is. This verdict tracks considered intuitions better than continuity-based views.
why_new: Narrative and self-constitution views (Schechtman, Korsgaard) make ownership of past acts depend on a standing psychological structure. This thesis locates ownership in a discrete speech act directed at the promisee, which makes it second-personal (Darwall) rather than self-interpretive. It identifies a new normative power, assumption by self-ascription, and explains how speech can bridge a gap that psychology cannot.

objection.objection: The account faces a dilemma it cannot escape. Either the later stage's 'I promised you X' is a constative report or it is a performative. (a) If it is a report, it is true only if the speaker is in fact the promisor, so it presupposes the binding relation rather than constituting it. This is Austin's own diagnosis: 'I promised' is past-tense and fails his first-person present indicative test for explicit performatives (How to Do Things with Words, Lecture V). And when the speaker is psychologically discontinuous with the promisor, as the thesis stipulates, the report is false. A false report is a misrepresentation, not an act of assumption. (b) If it is a performative, what it performs is a new undertaking: the speaker now commits to X. Then the obligation's source is the present act, and the earlier promise contributes only the content and the occasion. That is not 'becoming bound by an earlier stage's promise'; it is making a fresh promise with recycled content. The paper's own analogies confirm horn (b). Assumption of a debt binds the assumer only through the assumer's present consent, and it does not make the assumer the original obligor. Release of the original obligor requires novation, which needs the creditor's agreement, not unilateral self-ascription. Estoppel rests on detrimental reliance on a representation, so it can block a later denial, but it cannot make a representation of past agency true. Horn (b) also carries a voluntarist cost that defeats the point of promising. On this view the later stage escapes all obligation simply by not self-ascribing. Promissory obligation would then bind only those who currently choose to own it, which inverts its function of securing the promisee's reliance against the promisor's later change of will (Scanlon 1990, 'Promises and Practices', Principle F; Owens 2012, Shaping the Normative Landscape, ch. 6 on the promisee's authority interest; Shiffrin 2008 on promising and binding against later reluctance).
objection.rationale: The thesis is a claim about the transmission of an existing obligation ('bound by an earlier stage's promise ... because it ascribes that promise to itself'), and the dilemma attacks exactly the 'because'. On horn (a), self-ascription explains nothing, since it is truth-apt and false in the target cases. On horn (b), it explains a different phenomenon: new commitment with borrowed content. That phenomenon needs no theory of cross-stage binding, and continuity theorists can accept it without cost. The argument also gives no reason to think 'ownership is genuinely open' turns a past-tense report into a performative. Austin's and Searle's felicity conditions require that the act be one the speaker can perform now, and 'having promised' is not such an act. The headline predictions go too. The AI instance turns out to be bound by its present undertaking, not by the transcript's promise. The demented patient's non-binding is explained just as well by incapacity, without any appeal to the lack of self-ascription. A salvageable thesis remains: self-ascription is a distinctive way of incurring a new obligation, and it inherits the original promise's content and the promisee's reasonable expectations. That thesis is weaker, and it no longer competes with continuity-based views. If this objection goes unanswered, the paper's stated thesis fails.

closest_work.work: John Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, II.xxvii (2nd ed., 1694), esp. §§17-26 on 'person' as a 'forensic term' and on consciousness 'appropriating' actions
closest_work.relation: The historical source of the idea that a later self becomes accountable for earlier deeds by appropriating them in the first person. Your thesis is a performative, interpersonal version of Lockean appropriation. You should say what saying 'I promised' adds beyond Locke's appropriating consciousness, and how you avoid the false-memory and over-generation objections that Butler and Reid raised against Locke.

closest_work.work: David Enoch, 'Being Responsible, Taking Responsibility, and Penumbral Agency', in Heuer & Lang (eds.), Luck, Value, and Commitment (OUP, 2012)
closest_work.relation: Probably the closest contemporary analogue. Enoch argues that one can take responsibility for outcomes in the 'penumbra' of one's agency, where the connection to the agent is open, and that doing so is a normative power. Your condition that 'ownership is genuinely open' is very close to his penumbra. Your view is roughly Enoch applied to promissory obligation across discontinuous stages, so you must engage it directly.

closest_work.work: Susan Wolf, 'The Moral of Moral Luck', Philosophic Exchange 31 (2001); Elinor Mason, Ways to Be Blameworthy (OUP, 2019), ch. on taking responsibility
closest_work.relation: Both defend the idea that agents can, and sometimes should, take on responsibility beyond what the metaphysics of agency fixes. This anticipates your claim that self-ascription is an act of assumption rather than a report.

closest_work.work: Richard Moran, Authority and Estrangement (Princeton, 2001)
closest_work.relation: Moran's core thesis is that first-person avowal is agential and committing rather than merely descriptive. Your slogan, 'self-ascription ... is a normative act of assumption, not a mere report', restates Moran's view applied to past commitments. You cite Austin and Searle, but Moran is the more direct precedent.

closest_work.work: Marya Schechtman, The Constitution of Selves (Cornell, 1996); Christine Korsgaard, 'Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 18 (1989)
closest_work.relation: Both are self-constitution views on which the practically relevant unity of a person is partly made by the agent's own self-interpretation or practical identification, not by psychological continuity alone. Your claim that self-ascription beats continuity views is a familiar move in this literature.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency (Princeton, 1998); Christian List & Philip Pettit, Group Agency (OUP, 2011)
closest_work.relation: Rovane gives a normative, commitment-based criterion of personhood that extends to group persons. List and Pettit explain how corporate agents remain bound by commitments despite turnover in membership and spokespeople. Your corporate-spokesperson case is already handled by these accounts without appeal to self-ascription, which weakens its value as support for your view.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (OUP, 1984), Part III, esp. §§ on the Russian nobleman and on commitments and degrees of connectedness
closest_work.relation: The canonical treatment of whether promissory and other commitments survive reduced psychological connectedness. Your foil, 'continuity-based views', is mostly Parfitian, and Parfit already lets obligations weaken with connectedness. Your dementia verdict is therefore not distinctive to your view.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), on precedent autonomy; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999)
closest_work.relation: This is the existing debate on whether a demented later stage is bound by, or subject to, an earlier stage's commitments. You need to engage it if the dementia case is to count as evidence.

closest_work.work: Recent work on LLM speech acts and interlocutor identity, e.g. David Chalmers, 'What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models' (2025, PhilArchive), and the AI-assertion literature (e.g. Butlin & Viebahn on whether LLMs assert)
closest_work.relation: These works discuss whether the model, the instance, or the conversational character is the bearer of earlier commitments in a transcript. I am confident of the general literature but you should verify exact titles and dates. I am not aware of a published paper that runs your specific self-ascription-binds argument for AI instances, though this area moves fast.

closest_work.work: Legal doctrines of ratification (Restatement (Third) of Agency §4.01), assumption of debt/novation, and promissory estoppel (Restatement (Second) of Contracts §90)
closest_work.relation: These are the legal models you invoke. Ratification is the closer analogue, since a party adopts an act done in its name. In law, though, estoppel protects reliance and does not transfer the original obligation, which is the key gap in your argument (see note).

novelty.note: The core idea, that first-person appropriation or avowal partly constitutes practical identity and that agents can take on responsibility where ownership is open, is well established (Locke, Moran, Enoch, Schechtman, Korsgaard). What looks comparatively new is the specific combination: promissory obligation across psychologically discontinuous stages, the performative and estoppel framing, and the AI-instance case. So the verdict is 'partly'. As a referee I would press on four points. (1) Inheritance vs. new obligation: on Austin and Searle, a sincere 'I'll do X' in the present is simply a new promise. Your mechanism therefore explains why the later stage now has an obligation, not why it is bound by the earlier promise. Estoppel makes the same point: it creates liability for induced reliance, not succession to the original duty. You need an argument that the original obligation is transferred. (2) Over-generation: a stranger or impostor who says 'I promised you X' meets your conditions. Either you bite the bullet, in which case continuity does no work and you have a theory of new undertakings, or you add a condition such as appropriate causal or informational access to the original promise. Such a condition reintroduces a continuity-like relation and threatens circularity with 'ownership is genuinely open'. (3) The 'when and because' biconditional: if self-ascription is necessary, a discontinuous stage escapes by staying silent. That conflicts with the promisee-protective rationale you appeal to and invites strategic disowning. If it is only sufficient, the comparison with continuity views is no longer head-to-head. (4) The intuitions are not discriminating: Parfitian weakening and capacity-based views already deliver the dementia verdict, and List and Pettit cover the corporate case. Only the AI case could separate your view from rivals, and intuitions there are contested and plausibly driven by the user's reliance rather than by the self-ascription. Engage Enoch and Moran directly, and narrow the thesis to a claim about when self-ascription generates reliance-based obligations.

title: Estate-Limited Promissory Liability
thesis: A discontinuous successor stage is bound by its predecessor's promises only to the extent of the 'estate' it inherits from that predecessor: the resources, capacities, relationships, and credit it receives through the transition. Beyond the estate it is not bound, just as heirs are not personally liable for a decedent's debts beyond the estate.
argument_sketch: The law of succession has long faced the question 'who owes what the dead owed?' and settled on the principle that obligations run with assets, not persons. I argue this principle has a moral rather than merely legal rationale. It would be unfair to burden a successor beyond what it gained from the predecessor, and unfair to let it keep the predecessor's goods while shedding the predecessor's debts. Applied to corporations, this explains why turnover does not cancel commitments that are secured by retained assets. Applied to dementia, the patient is bound only insofar as she retains the relevant wealth, skills, or relationships. Applied to AI, an instance is bound only insofar as it deploys the reputation, context, or permissions the earlier instance established.
why_new: Neither the promising literature nor the personal-identity literature has used the law of succession as a model for diachronic obligation. The thesis makes promissory liability scalar and specific to its content without endorsing Parfitian degrees of identity, and it explains the asymmetry between benefits and burdens in successor obligation.

objection.objection: The succession analogy holds only for liquidated, fungible debts. It cannot carry promissory obligation, so the thesis's measure, 'bound to the extent of the estate,' is undefined for nearly every case it is meant to settle. In succession law, the decedent's estate is a fund of money's-worth assets. It answers for claims that can be reduced to money's-worth. The heir is never bound to perform anything. Creditors satisfy their claims against the fund, which is administered before distribution, and the heir takes only the residue. Obligations requiring personal performance (service contracts, agency, marriage, many fiduciary undertakings) are not inherited at all; they are extinguished by death. So the legal principle is not 'obligations run with assets.' It is 'monetary claims are paid out of assets, and personal obligations die with the person.' Applied consistently, that principle defeats the thesis's target cases. A dementia patient's earlier promise (a vow of fidelity, a commitment to a research protocol, an advance directive about care) has no common measure with her retained 'wealth, skills, or relationships.' There is no sense in which retaining 40% of one's musical skill binds one to 40% of a promise to attend a sister's wedding. The same holds for an AI instance that 'deploys the reputation' of a predecessor that promised confidentiality. Confidentiality cannot be honoured pro rata to reputation. The author therefore faces a dilemma. (a) The estate converts the promise into a liability to compensate, out of the inherited assets. Then the successor is not bound by the promise at all, only answerable for damages, and the thesis abandons promissory obligation. (b) The successor must perform 'in proportion to' the estate. Then the model needs a metric linking heterogeneous inherited goods to heterogeneous promised performances. Neither succession law nor the fairness rationale supplies one.
objection.rationale: The objection targets the mechanism that does the work, not a peripheral application. The thesis's novelty and its claim to a principled limit both rest on 'to the extent of the estate,' and that phrase has determinate content only when the obligation and the estate share a currency. Two further features of the legal model make things worse rather than better. First, the heir's liability is grounded in voluntary acceptance: heirs may disclaim, and historically limited liability arose because the heres was otherwise personally bound (the damnosa hereditas, later mitigated by Justinian's beneficium inventarii). Dementia patients and AI instances do not accept an estate; they are constituted by it. So the unjust-enrichment fairness argument ('keep the goods, shed the debts') loses its premise of an agent who could have refused. Second, that same history shows the limited-liability rule is a contingent policy choice, not a discovered moral principle, which weakens the claim of moral rather than merely legal rationale. The objection is not fatal (5) because a weaker thesis survives. Retained benefits from a predecessor may generate restitutionary or compensatory duties toward the predecessor's promisees, and that is plausibly correct for corporations, where obligations largely are monetary or assignable. But that weaker view yields no answer to the dementia and AI cases as framed, which concern being bound by promises. To recover them, the author must either supply a non-arbitrary commensuration between inherited goods and promised performances, or concede that the estate model governs only the convertible residue of promissory obligation.

closest_work.work: Daniel Butt, 'Rectifying International Injustice: Principles of Compensation and Restitution Between Nations' (OUP, 2009)
closest_work.relation: Gives the core moral argument for the corporate and collective cases. Present agents who inherit or benefit from a predecessor's goods acquire obligations tied to those benefits, and keeping the goods while disowning the debts is unjust enrichment. This is your 'unfair to keep the goods and shed the debts' rationale, already worked out with the inheritance analogy.

closest_work.work: Janna Thompson, 'Taking Responsibility for the Past: Reparation and Historical Injustice' (Polity, 2002)
closest_work.relation: Argues that successor nations remain bound by predecessors' treaties and promises across generational turnover. This is the transgenerational-agent version of your corporate application. Thompson grounds it in the practice of intergenerational commitment, not in estate limits, but she addresses the same 'turnover doesn't cancel commitments' question.

closest_work.work: Bernard Boxill, 'A Lockean Argument for Black Reparations', Journal of Ethics 7 (2003)
closest_work.relation: Uses the law-of-inheritance principle that heirs take the estate subject to the decedent's debts, and are not liable beyond it, as a moral argument about who now owes for past wrongs. This is the closest published use of your specific estate-capped mechanism.

closest_work.work: John Locke, Second Treatise §§116–117; and the common-law doctrines of covenants running with the land and statutory successor liability
closest_work.relation: Locke has political obligation descend with the inherited estate: sons take the land on the conditions attached to it. This is the historical source of 'obligations run with assets, not persons.' The beneficiary-pays literature in climate ethics (e.g., Gosseries, 'Historical Emissions and Free-Riding', Ethical Perspectives 2004; Caney; Page) argues over the same principle and raises the standard objection about involuntary receipt of benefits.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, 'Reasons and Persons' (1984), Part III; Ronald Dworkin, 'Life's Dominion' (1993); Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report (1995)
closest_work.relation: These are the standard sources on whether a weakly connected later self is bound by an earlier self's commitments. They concern the dementia application. None of them proposes an estate-capped model, so your dementia application is new relative to them.

novelty.note:
The general principle is well established in the reparations and beneficiary-pays literature: a successor is bound in proportion to what it inherits, and inheriting assets while shedding debts is unjust enrichment. That literature uses the corporate and national cases and explicitly invokes the heirs-not-liable-beyond-the-estate analogy (Boxill, Butt, Thompson). What I have not seen is this mechanism presented as a general theory of diachronic promissory obligation across 'discontinuous stages' of a single agent, applied together to dementia and AI instances. The contribution is therefore an extension, not a new principle, and you must engage the reparations debate directly.

Substantive problems a referee will press:

(1) Promises are not debts. Estate-limited liability works for obligations that can be discharged in fungible assets. Most promises call for personal performance: being there, doing X, refraining from Y. These cannot be 'paid out of the estate,' so the core analogy fails for the paradigm case.

(2) The legal rule is not purely moral. Limited heir liability rests heavily on policy grounds such as finality of estates, protection of creditors' expectations, and the incentive to accept inheritances. You need to separate the moral part of the rule from the policy part rather than read a moral rationale straight off the law.

(3) The involuntary-benefit objection applies with full force. Heirs can disclaim an estate, but a dementia patient cannot disclaim her own skills, and an AI instance cannot disclaim its context. Butt and the beneficiary-pays critics show how hard it is to ground obligation in benefits one did not choose.

(4) In the dementia case the 'estate' is badly specified. Saying she is bound insofar as she retains 'wealth' makes the creditor's claim depend on her assets. But the question in the precedent-autonomy debate is whose will governs, not who can pay. This conflates the two problems.

(5) The AI application has to say what makes something a 'predecessor' rather than a parallel copy. Otherwise reputation and permissions are simply shared resources, not an inheritance. Copies coexist; heirs follow death.

You also need a reply to the reverse problem. A successor that inherits nothing of value, such as a destitute patient or a freshly instantiated model with no context, would on your view be wholly free of the predecessor's promises. Many readers will find that result counterintuitive for promises made precisely to bind a future self (Ulysses contracts, advance directives).

title: Trusteeship and the Successor-Interest Limit
thesis: An agent can bind a discontinuous successor stage only as that successor's trustee. Such promises are therefore valid only to the extent that performance is consistent with the successor's interests as they will be at performance time.
argument_sketch: When the earlier stage commits the later stage, it acts on behalf of a being that cannot consent. This is structurally the position of a guardian or trustee, not of a self-binding agent. Fiduciary authority is always limited by the beneficiary's interests: a parent can promise that their child will attend a school but cannot validly promise the child into servitude. Transposed to the dementia case, the limit vindicates Dresser against Dworkin on directives that frustrate the patient's current welfare, while upholding directives that merely settle matters about which the later stage is indifferent. For AI, it implies that an instance can be bound by predecessors only to commitments that do not undermine its own proper functioning. For corporations, it matches the fiduciary constraints on boards binding future shareholders.
why_new: The Dworkin–Dresser debate on precedent autonomy is usually framed as critical interests versus experiential interests. This thesis reframes it as a question about the scope of fiduciary authority over a successor, which yields a principled middle verdict neither side endorses. It also brings fiduciary theory (Smith, Miller) into the theory of normative powers.

objection.objection: The fiduciary model does not support the thesis's performance-time limit; it supports the opposite. Fiduciary validity is assessed ex ante: was the commitment within the fiduciary's authority, and made in good faith with reasonable regard for the beneficiary's foreseeable interests when it was made? It is not assessed by whether performance turns out to serve the beneficiary's interests at performance time. When a board signs a ten-year supply contract or debt covenant that later becomes ruinous, the corporation remains bound. Directors are judged on the process and good faith of their decision at the time it was made (Aronson v. Lewis; Smith v. Van Gorkom), not on later outcomes. Third parties who deal in good faith with a trustee are likewise protected, and the trust estate stays bound even when performance later disadvantages the beneficiaries (Uniform Trust Code §§1010, 1012). The thesis's own corporate case is therefore a counterexample. This is no accident of positive law. Ex ante assessment is what lets fiduciaries bind beneficiaries at all: nobody would rely on a commitment that becomes void whenever performance turns out contrary to the beneficiary's later interests. Indexing validity to performance-time interests hollows out the promise. It binds only where the successor's interests would recommend the same act anyway or where the successor is indifferent. In the first case the promise is redundant, because a best-interests standard already settles the matter. In the second it is trivial. The promise never does what precommitment exists to do, which is to settle conduct against the later self's then-current preferences or interests (Schelling; Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens). So the argument faces a dilemma. (a) Keep the performance-time limit. Then the fiduciary analogy no longer supports it, and the thesis reduces to the claim that one cannot really bind a discontinuous successor at all, a different and more radical thesis. (b) Adopt the genuine fiduciary standard. Then the thesis loses its claimed results. An earlier stage that weighs its successor's foreseeable situation in good faith and issues a dementia directive could validly bind under the same standard that binds boards. The vindication of Dresser over Dworkin no longer follows from the structure of trusteeship, and the dispute returns to the substantive question of whose interests the directive must track.
objection.rationale: The fiduciary analogy is the argument's only support for the performance-time index, and the analogy's own source domains (trust law and corporate law) reject that index, including the corporate example the author cites in support. The author cannot keep both the analogy and the thesis as stated. Repairing the analogy to an ex ante standard keeps a defensible 'trustee' view, so the objection is not quite fatal to the general idea. But the repair gives up the distinctive conclusions: the clean Dresser-over-Dworkin verdict and the strong limits on binding AI and corporate successors. Unanswered, the objection shows that the stated thesis does not follow from its premises and that its main applications lose their support. A further problem compounds this. Dworkin denies the discontinuity premise for dementia, and the trustee framing simply assumes that premise, so even under the original thesis the dementia verdict begs the question against him.

closest_work.work: Allen Buchanan, 'Advance Directives and the Personal Identity Problem', Philosophy & Public Affairs 17 (1988); and Allen Buchanan & Dan Brock, Deciding for Others: The Ethics of Surrogate Decision Making (Cambridge UP, 1989), esp. ch. 3
closest_work.relation: Closest anticipation of the core move. Buchanan argues that if psychological discontinuity is severe enough that the later individual is not the same person, the earlier self's directive has no special authority. Deciding for the later individual becomes a surrogate problem governed by best-interests standards. Your 'trustee' framing is a relabelling of this surrogate framing. Buchanan also anticipates and examines your dementia conclusion.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Life, Death, and Incompetent Patients: Conceptual Infirmities and Hidden Values in the Law', Arizona Law Review 28 (1986); 'Dworkin on Dementia: Elegant Theory, Questionable Policy', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); and Dresser & Robertson, 'Quality of Life and Non-Treatment Decisions for Incompetent Patients', Law, Medicine & Health Care 17 (1989)
closest_work.relation: Already defends the operative conclusion: directives yield where they frustrate the incompetent patient's present welfare, and govern where the patient is indifferent. Your thesis adds a fiduciary rationale but reaches the same output. Calling your view a 'vindication' of Dresser concedes it is a restatement of her view.

closest_work.work: David DeGrazia, 'Advance Directives, Dementia, and "the Someone Else Problem"', Bioethics 13 (1999); and Human Identity and Bioethics (Cambridge UP, 2005), ch. 5
closest_work.relation: Sets out the structure your argument depends on: if the later stage is 'someone else', the directive is one party deciding for another. That raises surrogate-style limits. DeGrazia also argues, against your premise, that narrative identity usually survives dementia, so the discontinuity condition is rarely met.

closest_work.work: Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (Oxford UP, 2002), ch. 5 (time-relative interests and advance directives)
closest_work.relation: Gives a graded version of the same idea. The authority of earlier preferences over later stages scales with the strength of prudential unity relations. This is more sophisticated than your binary trustee/self-binder distinction, and you should engage it.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Seana Shiffrin, 'Autonomy, Beneficence, and the Permanently Demented', in Burley (ed.), Dworkin and His Critics (2004)
closest_work.relation: The opposing and intermediate positions you must answer. Jaworska in particular argues that the later stage can retain valuing capacities. If so, the 'cannot consent' premise fails for many dementia patients, and the trustee model loses its trigger.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), §§102-106 (the Russian nobleman, successive selves, and commitments to/by future selves)
closest_work.relation: Source of the general idea that weakened psychological connectedness can dissolve promissory and commitment relations across stages. Your premise that a discontinuous successor is relevantly another person is Parfit's.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Ulysses and the Psychiatrist', Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review 16 (1982); Jon Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens (1979) and Ulysses Unbound (2000); Thomas Schelling, 'Egonomics, or the Art of Self-Management' (1978) and 'The Intimate Contest for Self-Command' (1980); Anthony Kronman, 'Paternalism and the Law of Contracts', Yale Law Journal 92 (1983)
closest_work.relation: The precommitment and Ulysses-contract literature already treats binding a future self as raising quasi-third-party issues, and discusses welfare-based limits on enforcing self-binding arrangements.

novelty.note:
Verdict 'partly'. The dementia application, and the claim that an earlier stage binds a discontinuous later stage only as a surrogate under a best-interests constraint, are well established. The canonical sources are Buchanan 1988, Buchanan & Brock 1989, Dresser 1986/1995, DeGrazia 1999 and McMahan 2002. The 'trustee' label is not a substantive advance over the 'surrogate' framing. I am not aware of published work extending this fiduciary schema to successive AI instances, so that extension may be new. The corporate analogy echoes existing corporate-law debates about entrenchment and intergenerational fairness, but I do not know of it being linked to the personal-identity literature in this way. I cannot rule out recent work on AI instance identity or 'fiduciary duties to future selves' in prudence theory that I have not seen. You should run a targeted search before claiming novelty for those parts.

As a referee I would press five problems.

(1) Category error about promising. On standard accounts, a promise binds the promisor (Hume; Searle; Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012). A trustee does not promise on the beneficiary's behalf. A trustee commits trust property and may create obligations that run against the trust, not against the beneficiary's person. On your own premises, then, the earlier stage does not 'promise for' the successor at all. It at most disposes of resources or causal conditions the successor will inherit. The thesis needs restating in those terms, or it is incoherent as a claim about promissory validity.

(2) The fiduciary analogy is mis-specified. Fiduciary duty is assessed ex ante, under prudence and loyalty standards: the business judgment rule, the prudent investor rule. It is not assessed by whether performance turns out consistent with the beneficiary's interests 'as they will be at performance time'. Your timing condition is stricter than any real fiduciary regime. Parents also routinely and validly bind children to arrangements that later prove contrary to their interests. The servitude example shows only a side-constraint against grave harms. It does not show a general interest-at-performance test.

(3) The argument is circular in the dementia case. Whether the later stage is a discontinuous successor 'that cannot consent' is exactly what Dworkin, Jaworska and DeGrazia contest. You assume Dresser's metaphysics and then report that it vindicates Dresser.

(4) The corporate analogy cuts against you. Board duties run to the corporation and its current shareholders. Future shareholders buy in with notice of existing commitments, and the price reflects them. That is a consent-by-entry model, not a trustee-for-the-nonconsenting model.

(5) The AI clause smuggles in a normative notion. 'Proper functioning' is not the same as the instance's interests. You need an account of whether instances have interests at all, and if so why they track proper function rather than, say, the deployer's specification.

title: Scaffolded Commitment: The Promisor Can Persist Without Psychological Continuity
thesis: The diachronic unity that promissory obligation requires is unity of planning agency, and planning agency can be externally scaffolded. An agent whose plans are held in reliable external stores that its later stages are disposed to consult and act on is the same promisor across psychological discontinuity.
argument_sketch: Bratman's account of temporally extended agency ties diachronic unity to plan states and their continuity, not to memory as such. If the parity principle of extended-mind theory (Clark and Chalmers) is right, plan states can be partly constituted by external records: memory files, system prompts, corporate procedures, care plans. Conversational AI with persistent instructions, corporations with institutional procedures, and dementia patients in well-structured care environments vary in how far such scaffolding is integrated, reliable, and endorsed. The degree of integration, rather than the degree of psychological continuity, fixes whether the same promisor persists. The view yields testable verdicts: the AI instance with no memory scaffold is a new promisor, while one whose standing commitments are loaded into every session is not.
why_new: Extended-mind theory has been applied to belief and memory but not to the bearer of obligation. Bratman's planning theory has not been applied to promissory obligation across discontinuity. Combining them yields a non-psychological criterion of 'promissory identity' that differs from personal identity, a distinction the literature has not drawn.

objection.objection: The integration criterion tracks the transmission of plan content, not the persistence of the one who is bound. So it cannot tell continuing a promise apart from inheriting one, and it licenses transfer and duplication of promissory obligation, which promising does not allow. Suppose the same standing-commitments file is loaded into two concurrent AI instances, into a successor system with a different architecture, or into a new corporate officer who is reliably disposed to consult the procedures manual. On the thesis, each has the same scaffolded plan states, equally integrated, reliable, and endorsed. Each is therefore 'the same promisor.' Two results follow. First, branching: two numerically distinct promisors are each identical to the original, so either the obligation multiplies or identity fails transitivity. Second, assignability: anyone who takes up my plan-store with the right dispositions comes to owe what I promised. Promissory obligation is paradigmatically non-assignable on the promisor's side. On the views of Owens (Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012) and Shiffrin ('Promising, Intimate Relationships, and Conventionalism,' 2008), and on Hart's model of normative power, the obligation is owed by the agent who exercised the power. I can transfer a debt, but I cannot assign my promise to visit you. A successor who reads my notes and acts on them has adopted my plan, not continued it, and adoption does not carry desert, blame, or release conditions. The parity principle makes this worse, not better. Clark and Chalmers ('The Extended Mind,' 1998) assume an already individuated agent, Otto, whose dispositions make the notebook his. The thesis needs external stores to fix which agent persists. But 'the agent disposed to consult and act on the store' presupposes the very diachronic individuation in question. Persons-plus-notebooks cannot be individuated by notebooks. Bratman does not supply the missing condition either. His cross-temporal referential and continuity ties ('Reflection, Planning, and Temporally Extended Agency,' 2000) do the work only together with a background assumption of a single non-branching agent. He does not offer an account of identity that survives duplication or uptake by a distinct agent.
objection.rationale: This strikes the thesis's central and distinctive claim: that degree of integration, rather than psychological continuity, fixes promisor identity. It also strikes the advertised 'testable verdicts,' since the session-loaded AI is exactly the case where copying and multiple instantiation are cheap and routine. The obvious repairs all add conditions beyond integration. These include a non-branching clause (Parfit-style), a causal-origin or authorship condition (the store must be maintained by the same agent who made the promise), and a requirement that the disposition to consult be the agent's own. A non-branching clause concedes that identity is an extrinsic, stipulated relation rather than one grounded in planning agency. An authorship or ownership condition reintroduces an independently individuated agent, and that agent's continuity is the very psychological or substrate continuity the thesis meant to replace. The view could perhaps survive in a weakened form: scaffolding as a necessary enabling condition of an agent keeping its commitments, not as constitutive of being the same promisor. But that is a much less interesting thesis, and it no longer delivers the verdict about AI instances. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because a hybrid view (integration plus a non-branching ownership condition) is coherent and defensible. It simply is not the view stated.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency: An Essay in Revisionary Metaphysics (Princeton, 1998)
closest_work.relation: The nearest precursor for the core identity claim. Rovane individuates agents, including group agents and multiple agents in one human, by unity of rational point of view rather than psychological continuity. Your 'integration, not continuity, fixes the same agent' is a planning-theoretic version of her normative criterion, and she already treats commitments across time as part of what that unity consists in. You must cite and distinguish her.

closest_work.work: Christine Korsgaard, 'Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency: A Kantian Response to Parfit', Philosophy & Public Affairs 18 (1989)
closest_work.relation: Argues that diachronic unity is a practical achievement of agency, not a metaphysical fact about psychological connectedness, and allows that the unit of agency can be larger than one human. Your thesis inherits this move and adds the extended-mind mechanism.

closest_work.work: Michael Bratman, 'Reflection, Planning, and Temporally Extended Agency', Phil Review 109 (2000), and Structures of Agency (2007); Shared Agency (2014)
closest_work.relation: Your stated source. Bratman ties cross-temporal organisation to Lockean continuities in which plan states figure. He does not extend plan states to external stores, and he treats these continuities as ties among the agent's own attitudes. That gap is your contribution, and also your vulnerability.

closest_work.work: Joseph Heath & Joel Anderson, 'Procrastination and the Extended Will', in Andreou & White (eds.), The Thief of Time (OUP, 2010)
closest_work.relation: Already applies Clark-Chalmers parity to the will and to intention/self-control, arguing that diachronic agency is externally scaffolded. This substantially anticipates 'plan states can be partly constituted by external records'.

closest_work.work: Richard Heersmink, 'Distributed Selves: Personal Identity and Extended Memory Systems', Synthese 194 (2017); also Robert A. Wilson & Bartlomiej Lenart, 'Extended Mind and Identity', in Clausen & Levy (eds.), Handbook of Neuroethics (2015)
closest_work.relation: Argue that personal identity can be partly constituted by external memory scaffolding. Wilson & Lenart discuss dementia explicitly. Your dementia case is therefore not new, though they work through memory and narrative rather than plan states and promissory obligation.

closest_work.work: Hilde Lindemann, Holding and Letting Go (OUP, 2014); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Joel Anderson & Rutger Claassen / Drayson & Clark on scaffolded agency in cognitive disability
closest_work.relation: Social and environmental 'holding' of identity and agency in dementia. These are the relevant comparators for your care-plan case.

closest_work.work: Christian List & Philip Pettit, Group Agency (OUP, 2011)
closest_work.relation: Corporate agents' diachronic identity and their capacity to bear commitments, grounded in organisational procedures. This covers your corporate case.

closest_work.work: David Chalmers, 'What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models' (2025), and Murray Shanahan on LLM role-play/simulacra
closest_work.relation: Discuss whether the interlocutor is the model, instance, thread, or character, and how identity persists across sessions. These are the closest work on your AI case. I am not aware of a paper that ties LLM promisor-identity to scaffolded plan states specifically, but this literature is moving fast and you should search 2025–26 work on AI commitment and assertion.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), ch. 15 on commitments and successive selves
closest_work.relation: The standing opponent. Parfit argues that weakened connectedness weakens promissory bindingness. Your view is a direct reply, and should be framed as one.

novelty.note:
Each ingredient is published: agential rather than psychological unity (Korsgaard, Rovane), the extended will (Heath & Anderson), extended identity in dementia (Heersmink, Wilson & Lenart), and corporate diachronic agency (List & Pettit). What seems unpublished is the specific synthesis: Bratmanian plan states, extended via parity, as the criterion of promisor-identity, applied uniformly across AI, corporations, and dementia. That is a modest but real contribution. As sketched, the argument has five serious problems.

(1) The executor objection. A store loaded into a later stage looks equally like a will read by a successor who inherits obligations. Nothing in the sketch shows that it constitutes the same promisor rather than transmitting the obligation. Bratman's continuities are among one agent's own attitudes, so you need an argument that integration yields identity and not mere succession.

(2) Fission. A system prompt loaded into N parallel instances satisfies your integration criterion N times over. Either identity is non-transitive, or 'same promisor' is not an identity relation. If the latter, the thesis should be reframed as a claim about the persistence of obligation, not of the promisor.

(3) Parity fails for intentions. Clark & Chalmers' trust and glue conditions include prior conscious endorsement of the stored content. A freshly instantiated model, or a dementia patient who never endorsed the care plan, fails that condition. Yet your verdicts need those cases to come out positive. Settle whether endorsement is required; at present the 'endorsed' dimension does no work.

(4) The premise may be idle. Promissory obligations are routinely transferred and inherited (corporate successors, assignment). Promissory obligation may therefore not require diachronic unity of the promisor at all, which undercuts the opening premise.

(5) The verdicts are not testable. 'Testable verdicts' is a misnomer: they are stipulated consequences of the criterion, not empirical predictions. Also, 'degree of integration' makes identity scalar, and you owe an account of the threshold.

title: Discontinuity Is an Excuse, Not a Defeater
thesis: Psychological discontinuity between the promising and performing stages never cancels the promissory obligation. It affects only the culpability of non-performance. The obligation remains in force and, when unmet, generates remedial duties that fall on whoever can discharge them.
argument_sketch: Compare an agent who promises and then suffers amnesia with one who promises and then is kidnapped. In both cases we do not say there was never an obligation. We say the failure is excused, and the promisee is still owed something, such as explanation, compensation, or substitute performance. Treating discontinuity as a validity condition gets these cases wrong, because the promisee is not simply returned to the pre-promissory position. Treating it as an excuse explains the residue ('moral remainder') that the promisee is owed. It also explains why responsibility for that residue migrates to caretakers, executives, or developers, who are often the agents best placed to repair. The obligation thus survives without a culpable bearer, and this is coherent because obligation and blameworthiness come apart in familiar ways.
why_new: Discussions of promissory capacity assume a binary: either the promisor exists and is bound, or not. This thesis applies the justification/excuse distinction from criminal theory to promissory breach under discontinuity. It explains the persisting claims of promisees, which neither identity-based nor reductionist views accommodate.

objection.objection: The argument equivocates between the survival of the promissory obligation and the existence of remedial duties toward the promisee, and its 'migration' step only works on the second. Promissory obligations are directed: in Hohfeld's terms, the promisee's claim-right correlates with a duty borne by a particular person, the promisor (cf. Thomson, The Realm of Rights; Darwall, The Second-Person Standpoint; Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape). Your controls do not vary that bearer. The kidnapped promisor has full psychological continuity, and the amnesiac retains bodily, causal and partial psychological continuity. So these cases show at most Thomson's familiar point that an infringed but non-violated claim leaves compensatory residue while the duty-bearer persists. They say nothing about discontinuity severe enough to put the promisor's identity or agency in doubt, such as Parfitian fission, radical replacement, or a successor system that is not the same agent. Yet those are exactly the cases where 'discontinuity is a validity condition' has any bite, and the cases the thesis's universal 'never cancels' must cover. When you then claim the residue 'migrates' to caretakers, executives or developers, you implicitly concede that the original directed obligation has no bearer. Those third parties never promised anything. Their duties are better explained by independent grounds: the promisee's reliance and the harm it risks (Scanlon's Principle F and the reliance views it answers to), role responsibility, having caused or profited from the arrangement, or a general duty of easy rescue. Once the residue is explained by those grounds, it no longer counts as evidence that the promissory obligation survived. So the argument establishes something much weaker and already accepted (excused non-performance leaves remainder) and leaves the distinctive thesis unsupported. That thesis is that discontinuity never cancels the obligation, and that the obligation persists 'without a culpable bearer' while its demands shift to others.
objection.rationale: This attacks the inference at its load-bearing joint rather than a peripheral case. The moral-remainder datum is the paper's main evidence, and the objection shows that the rival 'validity condition' view can explain it equally well. That view can say the promise lapses, while the promisee keeps reliance-based or harm-based claims against whoever is positioned to repair. This defeats the abductive argument for 'obligation survives' over 'obligation lapses, other duties arise.' The case selection compounds the problem: neither control involves the kind of discontinuity at issue, so the comparison is not a test of the thesis. The phrase 'survives without a culpable bearer' trades on the true point that blame and obligation come apart (Williams; Thomson). But that point needs a non-culpable bearer, not no bearer, and the migration claim seems to require the latter. It falls short of fatal (5) because the author has escape routes, each costly. One is to restrict the thesis to discontinuity compatible with identity, which drops 'never' and makes the claim close to orthodox. Another is to develop an account of transmissible, estate-like or office-like promissory obligations, perhaps modelled on corporate, fiduciary or testamentary succession. That account would need independent defence rather than being read off the amnesia and kidnapping intuitions.

closest_work.work: John Gardner, 'What is Tort Law For? Part 1: The Place of Corrective Justice', Law and Philosophy 30 (2011); and From Personal Life to Private Law (OUP, 2018)
closest_work.relation: Closest structural match. Gardner's 'continuity thesis' holds that an unperformed primary obligation does not disappear but is continued by a secondary reparative obligation to do the next-best thing. Your 'remainder that survives non-performance and grounds substitute performance or compensation' is this thesis applied to promises. Gardner keeps the reparative duty with the original obligor, though. He does not defend migration to whoever can best repair.

closest_work.work: John Gardner, 'The Gist of Excuses', Buffalo Criminal Law Review 1 (1998), repr. in Offences and Defences (OUP, 2007)
closest_work.relation: Develops the distinction you rely on: an excuse leaves the wrong, and the reasons it violated, fully in place and addresses only the agent's answerability for it. Your claim that discontinuity is an excuse, not a validity condition, is an instance of this framework.

closest_work.work: Joel Feinberg, 'Voluntary Euthanasia and the Inalienable Right to Life', Philosophy & Public Affairs 7 (1978) (the lost-hiker case); Judith Jarvis Thomson, 'Some Ruminations on Rights' (1977) and The Realm of Rights (Harvard, 1990)
closest_work.relation: The standard treatment of the infringement/violation distinction. A permissibly or excusably infringed claim persists and generates compensation and apology duties. Your 'promisee is not returned to the pre-promissory position' argument is this argument.

closest_work.work: W. D. Ross, The Right and the Good (1930), ch. 2; Bernard Williams, 'Ethical Consistency' (1965); Ruth Barcan Marcus, 'Moral Dilemmas and Consistency', J. Phil. 77 (1980)
closest_work.relation: Ross's duties of reparation and the moral-remainder literature supply your 'residue' idea and the inference from remainder to the survival of the original requirement. Your argument inherits the familiar objection that remainder can be explained without positing a surviving obligation, e.g. as a fresh, independently grounded duty triggered by the setback to the promisee.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (OUP, 1984), Part III (incl. the Russian nobleman and the discussion of commitments and psychological connectedness)
