closest_work.relation: The locus classicus for the opposing view: reduced connectedness may weaken or dissolve commitments, which treats discontinuity as bearing on the obligation itself. You need to engage this directly. As it stands, your kidnapping analogy assumes away the very thing Parfit's view puts in question.

closest_work.work: David Shoemaker, 'Responsibility without Identity', Harvard Review of Philosophy 18 (2012); Andrew Khoury & Benjamin Matheson, 'Is Blameworthiness Forever?', Journal of the American Philosophical Association 4 (2018)
closest_work.relation: Recent work separating diachronic responsibility from strict identity. It is relevant to your claim that the culpability component tracks psychological relations while something else, on your view the obligation, does not.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); Hilde Lindemann, Holding and Letting Go (OUP, 2014)
closest_work.relation: The precedent-autonomy and dementia literature addresses whether earlier commitments bind a psychologically discontinuous later self, and what role caretakers play in sustaining them. This is the nearest existing discussion of your 'migration to caretakers' clause.

closest_work.work: Andreas Matthias, 'The Responsibility Gap', Ethics and Information Technology 6 (2004); Robert Sparrow, 'Killer Robots', J. Applied Philosophy 24 (2007); Filippo Santoni de Sio & Giulio Mecacci, 'Four Responsibility Gaps with AI', Philosophy & Technology 34 (2021); Daniel Tigard, 'There Is No Techno-Responsibility Gap', Philosophy & Technology 34 (2021)
closest_work.relation: The responsibility-gap literature already debates whether obligations or answerability can persist without a culpable bearer and be redistributed to developers or deployers. Your 'developers' extension enters this debate. It is not opening a new one.

novelty.note:
Most components are well established. These are: obligation survives excused non-performance; the survival grounds reparative duties; excuses bear on culpability, not on the wrong; and obligation comes apart from blameworthiness (Gardner, Feinberg/Thomson, Ross, Williams/Marcus). What is less clearly anticipated is the conjunction of (a) a universal claim that psychological discontinuity never voids promissory obligation with (b) a principle that remedial duties migrate to whoever is best placed to discharge them. I cannot rule out a recent paper making exactly this conjunction, so 'partly' is the safe verdict.

As a referee I would press four problems. First, the amnesia/kidnapping analogy is question-begging. Kidnapping leaves the promisor's identity untouched, while severe discontinuity is precisely what Parfitians claim may sever the normative relation to the promisor. Treating the two cases as parallel presupposes the conclusion. Second, 'never' is too strong. Promises carry implicit conditions, and contract law's frustration doctrine (Taylor v Caldwell, 1863) discharges, not excuses, obligations when performance becomes radically different. It leaves only restitution of benefits conferred (cf. the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943). So the 'remainder' can be explained without a surviving obligation, which is a direct counter-model to your inference. Third, the migration principle is unsupported. Gardner's continuity thesis keeps the secondary duty with the original obligor, and 'best placed to repair' is a Singer/Goodin-style capacity criterion that would make strangers liable for others' promises. You need a grounding relation, such as agency, guardianship, vicarious liability, or authorship of the system, and that relation, not the promise, will be doing the normative work. Fourth, 'an obligation without a culpable bearer' needs a bearer of some kind. If the post-discontinuity agent is not the obligor and the caretaker did not promise, you owe an account of whose obligation is 'in force'. Otherwise the view collapses into 'the promisee has a claim against no one in particular', which is a different and weaker thesis.

title: The Appropriation Condition: Why the AI Case and the Dementia Case Come Apart
thesis: A later stage is bound by an earlier stage's promise if and only if it has the capacity, at performance time, to take the promise as a reason of its own when presented with it. That capacity can be present without memory (memoryless AI) and absent despite continuity of organism (advanced dementia).
argument_sketch: Promissory obligation functions as a reason-giving relation: its point is that the promisor treats the promisee's claim as settling what to do. A stage that cannot so treat the claim cannot be bound in the relevant sense, because the obligation would be idle. A stage that can, when informed, is apt to be bound, since being given the record of one's commitment and recognizing it as a valid claim is how normative uptake works. A memoryless AI instance presented with a transcript can appropriate. A patient with advanced dementia often cannot, even with full narrative support. Hence the three standard cases sort differently than continuity theories predict, and the sorting matches considered judgments.
why_new: Jaworska's work on 'valuing' at the margins of agency addresses whether dementia patients retain agency, but not what that implies for prior commitments. Narrative views require self-interpretation over time. This thesis proposes a synchronic, capacity-based criterion that is externally triggerable, and argues that it, rather than any diachronic relation, is what promissory binding requires.

objection.objection:
The criterion cannot say whom the promise binds. It needs a relation tying the bound stage to the promise, and it can only get one by bringing back what it set out to replace. Take the phrase 'take the promise as a reason of its own.' Read it one of two ways.

(a) Thin reading: 'of its own' means only that the agent treats the promisee's claim as settling what it should do. Then nearly any competent reasoner handed the transcript qualifies: a stranger, a different AI model, a second instance spun up in parallel, the promisor's sibling. Nothing in the capacity separates the original promisor's successor from anyone else who can read and recognize claims. The thesis then says every such agent is bound, which is absurd. Promissory obligation is a directed, bipolar relation between this promisor and this promisee (Thompson, 'What Is It to Wrong Someone?'; Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012). Only the person who made the promise can owe it.

(b) Thick reading: 'of its own' means the agent recognizes the commitment as its own, as something it undertook. Then the criterion presupposes the ownership relation it was meant to explain. This is Butler's circularity objection to Locke, now aimed at practical rather than mnemonic appropriation. The AI case makes the problem sharp. A memoryless instance 'recognizing' a transcript as its own commitment is either (i) mistaken, if no further relation holds, or (ii) correct only because some independent relation does hold, such as same weights, same deployment, or a causal chain of instantiation. Any such relation is a continuity condition.

The author must also explain why the instance's appropriation is not just a fresh promise, or voluntary assumption of someone else's debt, rather than a case of being bound by the earlier promise. If it is a fresh promise, it reverses the thesis: a binding promise holds whether or not the promisor later endorses it.

On either reading, the claim that the cases 'sort differently than continuity theories predict' fails. On (a) the sorting overgenerates. On (b) it inherits continuity's verdicts.
objection.rationale:
Left unanswered, this defeats the thesis as a biconditional. The thin reading has decisive counterexamples (the stranger with the transcript), so the right-to-left direction fails. The thick reading is circular, so the thesis gives no independent criterion and cannot compete with continuity theories.

The obvious repair is to add a relational condition: the stage must stand in relation R to the promisor and also have the capacity. This makes capacity a necessary condition layered on continuity. That is a much weaker and largely familiar claim, close to Korsgaard's agency-based unity ('Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency,' 1989) or to Jaworska-style capacity conditions. It also gives up the headline result that memoryless AI is bound because of capacity alone.

The objection also exposes a second problem. The 'idleness' argument mistakes the bearer's responsiveness for the obligation's existence. Directed obligations can persist where the obligor cannot act on them, as with debts during incapacity or claims passed to guardians. So even the necessity direction rests on an unargued premise.

The appeal to 'considered judgments' does not rescue the argument. The AI verdict is the disputed point, not a datum. Dementia intuitions are divided, as the Dworkin vs. Dresser/Jaworska debate over precedent autonomy shows. The thesis cannot use these cases to fix the criterion while also using the criterion to settle the cases.

closest_work.work: Christine Korsgaard, 'Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency: A Kantian Response to Parfit', Philosophy & Public Affairs 18 (1989); developed in Self-Constitution (2009)
closest_work.relation: Closest structural precedent. Korsgaard grounds diachronic unity in the practical standpoint of a deliberating agent rather than in metaphysical continuity. Your thesis is a local, promise-specific version of the same move: practical uptake, not continuity, settles who is bound.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency (1998)
closest_work.relation: Argues that a person is individuated by a commitment to rational/normative unity, not by organism or memory. Rovane explicitly allows the agent-boundary to diverge from the organism-boundary in both directions. That is the same sorting your three cases rely on.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), esp. §§ on the Russian nobleman and on commitments and desert under reductionism
closest_work.relation: The locus classicus for the question of whether a later stage is bound by an earlier stage's commitment once identity is deflated. Your thesis answers Parfit's question with a uptake criterion instead of degrees of connectedness.

closest_work.work: David Shoemaker, 'Personal Identity and Practical Concerns', Mind 116 (2007)
closest_work.relation: Argues that distinct practical concerns (responsibility, compensation, self-concern) need not track a single identity relation. Your thesis is an instance of this pluralism applied to promissory obligation.

closest_work.work: Locke, Essay II.xxvii ('person' as a forensic term; appropriation through consciousness)
closest_work.relation: Your key verb, 'appropriate,' is Locke's. The novel element is decoupling appropriation from memory and making it a present-tense capacity triggered by testimony or record.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993); Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report (1995); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Seana Shiffrin, 'Autonomy, Beneficence, and the Permanently Demented' (2004)
closest_work.relation: The advance-directive/precedent-autonomy debate is the existing literature on whether an earlier self's commitment binds a demented later self. Jaworska's capacity-to-value criterion is a near neighbor to your capacity-to-appropriate criterion and cuts against your claim that advanced dementia typically lacks it.

closest_work.work: Hilde Lindemann, 'Holding One Another (Well, Wrongly, Clumsily) in a Time of Dementia', Metaphilosophy 40 (2009)
closest_work.relation: Narrative 'holding' by others as a way of sustaining identity in dementia. You claim narrative support is insufficient. That claim needs to engage her view directly.

closest_work.work: Stephen Darwall, The Second-Person Standpoint (2006); T. M. Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other (1998), ch. 7 (Principle F)
closest_work.relation: Supply the 'reason-giving relation' account of promissory obligation and the addressee-competence condition on accountability that your argument presupposes but does not cite.

closest_work.work: David Chalmers, 'What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models' (2025)
closest_work.relation: Recent treatment of what the bearer of commitments is in LLM interactions (model, instance, thread, character). It is the natural point of contact for your memoryless-AI case, though it does not state your biconditional.

novelty.note: The general strategy is well established: let a practical relation, not metaphysical continuity, fix who bears a commitment, and let the relevant unit diverge from the organism (Korsgaard, Rovane, Shoemaker). Applying it to dementia via a capacity criterion is also established (Jaworska, Shiffrin). I know of no published work that states your specific biconditional ('capacity at performance time to take the promise as one's own reason when presented with it') or that pairs the memoryless-AI case with dementia as a double dissociation. That pairing is the defensible contribution, but I cannot rule out recent AI-ethics papers. As a referee, I think the argument as sketched fails in three places. (1) Over-generation: any competent reasoner shown the transcript, including a stranger or a different AI instance, can recognize the claim as valid and act on it. Your criterion does not distinguish appropriating a promise as one's own from merely acknowledging that someone is owed something. That distinction is exactly the work continuity theories were doing, and you need a replacement. (2) 'Idle obligation' does not follow from lack of uptake. It conflates being bound with being responsive to the bond (cf. Williams on internal reasons and the externalist replies). The promisee's claim plausibly survives the promisor's incapacity and is redirected to guardians or the estate, which a reason-giving account can accommodate. (3) The biconditional lets an agent dissolve obligations by self-incapacitation, and 'considered judgments' about memoryless AI are not settled enough to serve as data. Engaging Jaworska, Lindemann, and Shoemaker 2007 is mandatory for publication.

title: The Reverse Priority Thesis: Discontinuous Promising Is the Paradigm
thesis: The practice of promising is functionally designed for securing future performance from agents whose motivational states cannot be relied upon to persist. Promising across psychological discontinuity is therefore the central case, and ordinary individual promising is a limiting case in which continuity happens to make the institutional supports redundant.
argument_sketch: Hume's account of promising as an artificial virtue explains promises as a remedy for the unreliability of future motivation. Discontinuity is the extreme of that unreliability. If promising's function is to bind an agent whose future self may not share present intentions, then the cases where the future stage shares nothing are where the function is most fully exercised, not where it fails. Corporate and treaty commitments, which outlive all their makers, are historically and structurally central to the practice of binding commitments. Theories that make personal identity a precondition of promising thus mistake an incidental feature of the simplest case for an essential feature of the practice. I show that practice-based accounts (Rawls, Kolodny and Wallace) are best read this way, and that this reading answers Owens's objection that practice views cannot explain bare promises.
why_new: The literature treats corporate and AI promising as derivative extensions to be explained by analogy with individual promising. This thesis inverts that priority on functional and genealogical grounds and draws the consequences for the debate between conventionalist and non-conventionalist theories of promising.

objection.objection: The argument equivocates between two kinds of unreliability. The first is unreliability of a persisting agent's future motivation. The second is the absence of any agent who is answerable for the commitment. Hume's remedy only addresses the first, and it works by exploiting continuity of the bearer. In Treatise 3.2.5, a promise works because the promisor 'subjects himself to the penalty of never being trusted again in case of failure.' Future performance is secured by attaching a sanction (reputational, and on practice views also normative and reactive) to the same bearer whose motivation may lapse. That mechanism needs someone who can later be held to account, distrusted, or blamed. Where the future stage 'shares nothing,' the lever has nothing to act on. That case is not the function exercised most fully. It is the case where the function cannot be discharged at all. A fire alarm's function is not 'most fully exercised' in a building with no occupants. The corporate and treaty cases confirm this rather than refute it. The doctrine of state continuity (and of state succession to treaties) and the legal personhood of corporations are artificial devices for constructing a persisting answerable bearer across turnover of members. Institutions do not make identity redundant. They manufacture a surrogate for it, precisely because commitment fails without one. So the institutional supports are not what is left of promising once the incidental feature of identity is removed. They are what the practice must build when natural identity is unavailable, which shows that a persisting locus of accountability is essential. This also undercuts the Owens payoff. Owens (Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012) presses that bare promises bind with no assurance interest and no practice-backed sanction in play. A view that makes institutional enforcement apparatus the central case makes bare promises more anomalous, not less. Bare promises become doubly peripheral: they are cases of continuity, and they are cases where the apparatus is idle.
objection.rationale: The objection targets the inference on which the whole thesis rests: from 'promising remedies motivational unreliability' to 'total discontinuity is the central case.' It does this using the very Humean text the author relies on. Unanswered, it does three things. It reverses the reading of the corporate and treaty evidence. It shows that the Rawls and Kolodny–Wallace practice views (Rawls 1955 and TJ §52; Kolodny & Wallace 2003) are better read as requiring a persisting answerable participant in the practice, not as dispensing with one. And it turns the reply to Owens into a liability. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because a fallback exists. The author could weaken the thesis to: what promising requires is a persisting bearer of accountability, which need not be a psychologically continuous person. That keeps the anti-psychological-continuity conclusion. But the fallback abandons the headline claim that discontinuity is the central case. It concedes that an identity-like relation (sanctionable continuity of the bearer) is essential rather than incidental. And it still owes an account of why manufactured bearers are the paradigm rather than a derivative extension of the individual case. So the paper as framed would not survive.

closest_work.work: Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 3.2.5 ('Of the obligation of promises')
closest_work.relation: Your source, but it cuts against you. Hume's problem is that the promisee cannot rely on the promisor's future benevolence or gratitude, not that the promisor's future self may share nothing with the present one. His mechanism also presupposes continuity: the promisor 'subjects himself to the penalty of never being trusted again in case of failure.' A reputational sanction needs a continuing bearer. On Hume's account, total discontinuity is where the artifice has nothing to act on, not where its function is 'most fully exercised.'

closest_work.work: Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III, esp. ch. 15 on commitments, desert and the Reductionist View; also the 'Russian nobleman' case (§ 80)
closest_work.relation: The canonical treatment of whether commitments survive weakened psychological connectedness. Parfit argues the reverse inference: reductionism plausibly weakens the force of past commitments as connectedness fades. Any claim that discontinuity is the central case must answer him directly. He is the obvious closest interlocutor and the sketch does not mention him.

closest_work.work: Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens (1979) and Ulysses Unbound (2000); Holmes, 'Precommitment and the Paradox of Democracy' (1988); Rubenfeld, Freedom and Time (2001)
closest_work.relation: These already develop 'binding a future self whose motivations cannot be relied on' as the core rationale of precommitment. They extend it, as you do, to constitutions and collective commitments that outlive their makers. Elster in Ulysses Unbound explicitly worries about whether intra-personal precommitment and constitutional precommitment are the same phenomenon, and concludes they largely are not. Your generalization from the individual case to the institutional case is exactly the move he scrutinizes.

closest_work.work: Bratman, Intention, Plans, and Practical Reason (1987) and Structures of Agency (2007)
closest_work.relation: Gives the standard functionalist account of future-directed commitment as a remedy for the unreliability of reconsideration. It ties that remedy to cross-temporal Lockean continuity rather than treating continuity as incidental. This is the rival functional story you need to defeat.

closest_work.work: List & Pettit, Group Agency (2011); Gilbert, Joint Commitment (2014) and A Theory of Political Obligation (2006)
closest_work.relation: The literature on corporate and collective commitment. It treats persisting group agents, held together by institutional rather than psychological continuity, as the bearers of obligations. This is the standard explanation of your corporate and treaty cases, and it does not dispense with identity. It relocates identity to the group agent.

closest_work.work: Rawls, 'Two Concepts of Rules' (1955) and A Theory of Justice §52; Kolodny & Wallace, 'Promises and Practices Revisited' (Philosophy & Public Affairs 2003)
closest_work.relation: The practice views you propose to reinterpret. Neither text frames promising's function in terms of discontinuity. Reading them that way would be a new interpretation, but you need textual support. K&W's account explicitly routes the wrong of promise-breaking through expectations a particular promisor has induced.

closest_work.work: Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape (2012), chs. 6–8; Shiffrin, 'Promising, Intimate Relationships, and Conventionalism' (Phil Review 2008)
closest_work.relation: Owens supplies the bare-promise objection. Shiffrin presses related worries that conventionalist and function-based views misidentify what is central to promising.

closest_work.work: Habib, 'Promises', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
closest_work.relation: A useful check of the survey literature. As far as I know, no published treatment advances your specific inversion, that discontinuous and institutional promising is central and individual promising is the limiting case.

novelty.note:
The ingredients are well established. Promising and precommitment as remedies for unreliable future motivation come from Hume, Elster and Bratman. Whether commitments survive discontinuity comes from Parfit. Group and treaty commitments come from List & Pettit and Gilbert. I know of no published defence of the specific inversion, so 'partly' rather than 'known'. I have not done an exhaustive search, and you should check recent work on collective and intergenerational promising before claiming priority.

As a referee I would flag four problems.

(1) The Hume reading is unsupported and arguably backwards, for the reasons given above.

(2) The corporate and treaty cases do not show that identity is incidental. They show that the identity of the obligor can be institutional rather than psychological. A corporation or state is a persisting bearer, which is precisely why pacta sunt servanda attaches to states rather than to signatories. The historical record also tells against you. Many pre-modern treaties were personal oaths of rulers that required renewal on succession. This suggests the practice treated discontinuity of the bound party as a defeater, not as the paradigm.

(3) 'Central case' and 'limiting case' are not doing clear work. You need either an etiological account of function (Millikan-style: what the practice was selected for), with historical evidence, or a conceptual-priority claim, with an argument. Frequency and maximal exercise of function are neither.

(4) The reply to Owens does not obviously follow. A bare promise is one with no reliance, no assurance interest and no practice benefit. Making institutional commitment central does nothing to explain why such a promise binds. If anything, a more thoroughly functionalist reading of Rawls and Kolodny & Wallace makes bare promises harder to explain, since their binding force must then come from the function, which is idle in those cases.

As it stands, the paper's novelty lies in a reframing whose main supports, the Hume reading and the institutional cases, are the weakest parts of the argument.

title: Promissory Novation: The Promisee's Power Replaces the Promisor's Identity
thesis: When a promisor's later stage is discontinuous, the original promise lapses, but the promisee acquires a normative power to accept the successor as substitute obligor (novation). The successor is bound if and only if both it and the promisee accept the substitution.
argument_sketch: In contract law, a debt cannot be transferred to a new debtor without the creditor's consent, because the creditor contracted with a particular obligor whose reliability mattered. Promising has the same structure: what the promisee relied on was that this agent would perform. Discontinuity breaks this, but it does not leave the promisee powerless. Because the promise was oriented toward the promisee's interests, it is the promisee who holds the power to decide whether continuation by a successor serves those interests. The view explains why some promisees feel betrayed by a 'new' corporate counterpart or AI instance and others do not. It also explains why the dementia patient's family, rather than the patient, often has the final say about the patient's earlier commitments to them.
why_new: The literature focuses on the promisor's powers (to bind, to retract) and on the promisee's power to release. It has not identified a promisee power of substitution. Novation brings a familiar legal mechanism into the philosophy of promising and shows that the role diachronic identity plays can be partly taken over by the promisee's normative authority.

objection.objection: The biconditional collapses novation into an ordinary new promise, and this leaves the promisee's supposed new normative power idle. On the thesis, the original promise has lapsed, and the successor is bound only if it accepts the substitution and the promisee accepts it too. But a successor's voluntary undertaking to perform for the promisee, taken up by the promisee, simply is a promise and its acceptance. It needs no prior power in the promisee and no residue of the old promise. In law, novation does real work because the original obligation still exists and is extinguished and replaced in one act. Here the original obligation has already lapsed, so there is nothing to novate. The 'power to accept the successor as substitute obligor' is therefore just the power any promisee has to accept a fresh offer. Worse, the explanatory payoffs require exactly what the biconditional rules out. (a) A promisee can be betrayed by a 'new' corporate or AI counterpart only if that counterpart was already bound before consenting. On the thesis, a non-accepting successor owes nothing, and an accepting one is bound by its own promise, so betrayal-as-breach of the original commitment is never available. (b) In the dementia case, the successor (the patient) typically cannot accept, so the thesis predicts the successor is not bound. Yet the case is offered as one where the family's decision settles the patient's earlier commitments, which is a unilateral power the biconditional explicitly denies. The family may also not be the promisee, which adds a third-party proxy the account has no room for.
objection.rationale: This does not touch the lapse claim. It does remove everything distinctive in the thesis. The author faces a dilemma. Keep successor consent, and the view reduces to 'old promise lapses; new promises can be made', which is true but trivial. The contract-law analogy and the interest-based grounding of the promisee's power then do no work, since standard accounts of promissory uptake (Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape; Raz on normative powers) already cover it. Drop successor consent to save the betrayal and dementia data, and the view needs a theory of how one agent can bind another without its consent. The debt-assignment analogy cannot supply this, because legal novation and delegation both require the new obligor's agreement. The legal analogy also cuts against the lapse premise. When a debtor dies, the closest legal analogue to discontinuity, the obligation does not lapse but runs against the estate, except for personal-performance contracts. That suggests the right model is either survival or personal-service extinction, not lapse plus novation. A revised view might rescue a non-trivial claim, for example that the successor's acceptance inherits the original terms, standing, and remedies rather than starting fresh. But that is a different thesis from the one stated, and it would need its own argument. Hence 4, not 5.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), esp. §§ on the Russian Nobleman (ch. 15) and on commitments under reduced psychological connectedness (ch. 15, 'Deserving Punishment' and 'Commitment')
closest_work.relation: Source of the premise that a promise may fail to bind a psychologically discontinuous later stage, and that what matters is connectedness rather than identity. Parfit also notes that the promisee, not the changed promisor, is positioned to release. He stops short of a transfer or substitution mechanism. The author's first clause, that the promise lapses under discontinuity, is essentially Parfit's view and needs no new argument. The novelty claim must rest on the second clause.

closest_work.work: David Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape (OUP 2012), chs. 6–9; also Seana Shiffrin, 'Promising, Intimate Relationships, and Conventionalism' (Phil Review 2008), and Gary Watson, 'Promises, Reasons, and Normative Powers' (2009)
closest_work.relation: The promisee's 'authority interest' and the promisee-held power of release are well established here. The submission's step from 'the promise serves the promisee's interests' to 'the promisee holds the power to accept a substitute' extends this release-power literature but is not argued for independently. Owens in particular denies that promissory authority is grounded in the promisee's first-order interests, which cuts against the author's grounding.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia' (Hastings Center Report 1995); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency' (PPA 1999); Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (2002), time-relative interests
closest_work.relation: Standard literature on whether an earlier self's commitments and directives bind a discontinuous later self with dementia. It is directly relevant to the author's dementia example. It frames the issue as precedent autonomy versus the current self's interests, not as promisee-held novation.

closest_work.work: Janna Thompson, Taking Responsibility for the Past (2002); Anna Stilz, 'Collective Responsibility and the State' (JPP 2011); Toni Erskine (ed.), Can Institutions Have Responsibilities? (2003)
closest_work.relation: Address whether successor states and corporations inherit predecessors' obligations, including promissory and treaty obligations, and under what continuity conditions. This is the natural home for the corporate-counterpart example. These works generally treat succession as automatic or continuity-conditioned, not as requiring both the successor's and the promisee's consent.

closest_work.work: Christine Korsgaard, 'Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency: A Kantian Response to Parfit' (P&PA 1989); Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency (1998)
closest_work.relation: Argue that the agent's commitments partly constitute diachronic identity, so the successor's acceptance is part of what makes it the same agent. A Korsgaardian will say the author's 'successor accepts' condition simply re-establishes agential continuity. On that reading this is not novation of a lapsed promise but its reinstatement.

closest_work.work: Doctrinal private law on novation and delegation of duties: Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§ 280, 318–328; Treitel/Peel, The Law of Contract, ch. on assignment; Andrew Tettenborn and others on the asymmetry between assignment of rights and transfer of burdens
closest_work.relation: The legal analogy is textbook. The creditor-consent requirement for substituting a debtor is standard doctrine, and the reliance on a particular obligor's identity is the standard rationale. I know of no work that imports novation as a model for promissory obligation across personal-identity discontinuity, though I have not checked exhaustively and recent AI-ethics literature on model versioning should be searched.

novelty.note:
The components are known: discontinuity defeats promissory obligation (Parfit), the promisee holds normative authority over the promise (Owens, Shiffrin, Watson), and novation requires creditor consent (black-letter law). The specific synthesis, a promisee-held power of novation conditional on lapse with a biconditional dual-consent condition, appears not to be published as such, so 'partly'. As referee I would press four problems.

(1) Incoherence of the mechanism. Legal novation extinguishes a subsisting obligation and replaces it. It presupposes that the original debt is valid at the moment of substitution. On the author's view the original promise has already lapsed, so there is nothing to novate. The 'power' is then a power over a nullity, and the author needs a separate account of what grounds it. 'The promise was oriented toward the promisee's interests' cannot do this work once the promise is gone.

(2) Collapse into a fresh promise. If the successor is bound iff it accepts and the promisee accepts, the result is indistinguishable from the successor making a new promise that the promisee takes up (Scanlon's Principle F, Gilbert's joint commitment). What does 'novation' add beyond a new promise with the same content? To earn the label, the author must show that some feature carries over from the original and would be absent in a fresh promise, such as priority, the original date of breach, or remedial entitlements.

(3) The dementia case does not fit. The family typically has the final say over the patient's commitments generally, including commitments to third parties. They do so as surrogates or proxies, not as promisees, so the phenomenon is better explained by surrogate decision-making (Buchanan & Brock, Deciding for Others, 1989). Where the family is the promisee, the author's view says the successor must also accept. A severely demented patient often cannot do so, which yields the wrong result: the family could not hold the patient to anything, yet the claimed datum is that they 'have the final say.'

(4) The betrayal datum underdetermines the view. Differential reactions to a 'new' corporate or AI counterpart are equally predicted by views that make succession automatic but defeasible, or that track reasonable expectations of continuity. The author must identify a case where only promisee-held novation gets the verdict right.

title: AI Cross-Session Commitments Are Warranties, Not Promises
thesis: When a conversational AI instance without persistent memory says it 'will' do something in a future session, it does not and cannot promise. It makes a warranty, an assertoric guarantee about the system's behavior, and it should be held to the norms of warranty rather than promissory norms.
argument_sketch: A promise binds the promisor to act. A warranty asserts that something will be so and allocates risk if it is not, without binding any agent's will. An AI instance's 'commitment' about a future session concerns the behavior of a system the instance does not control and with which it does not share agency. Its content is therefore best understood as a warranty that the deployment will behave as stated. The difference matters: warranty breach calls for compensation by whoever stands behind the warranty, typically the operator or developer, and not for the blame and apology appropriate to promissory breach. It also matters for sincerity, since an AI instance can sincerely warrant what it cannot sincerely promise. Treating such utterances as promises is a category error that produces misplaced blame and obscures responsibility.
why_new: Work on artificial agency (Floridi and Sanders, Nyholm) asks whether AI can be a moral agent at all. This thesis sidesteps that question by identifying a speech-act type that fits the case regardless of AI moral status. It imports the warranty/promise distinction from contract law to resolve the attribution problem for memoryless agents.

objection.objection: The incapacity argument that rules out promising rules out warranting just as thoroughly, and fixing it brings back promising. The argument says the instance cannot promise because the future session is behavior of a system it does not control and with which it shares no agency. But a warranty is not a free-floating assertion. It is an undertaking by a warrantor who assumes the risk of falsity and owes the remedy, which requires standing, continuity across the period of the guarantee, and something to answer with. The instance has none of these. So on the paper's own premises it cannot warrant either. The obvious repair is to say the operator or developer stands behind the warranty and the instance merely voices it. That makes the instance a representative speaking for a principal, like a sales clerk who says 'we will deliver on Tuesday' without controlling the delivery department. Such representative utterances are standardly analysed as promises made on behalf of the principal, binding through authority, not as non-promissory warranties. The control/shared-agency premise is therefore false as a condition on promising: one can promise through an agent who does not control the performance. And once the speech act is a representative promise, the paper's practical conclusion fails. Blame and apology are not misplaced. They are owed by the principal, just as a firm that breaks its salesperson's promise owes an apology and not merely compensation. The dilemma: either the instance is the warrantor (impossible by the paper's own reasoning) or the operator is (and then the utterance is a promise by proxy, not a warranty).
objection.rationale:
The objection hits all three load-bearing steps.

(1) The control premise. Agency law and ordinary practice both recognise promises made by agents who do not control performance (Restatement (Third) of Agency §§2.01–2.03, actual and apparent authority). Collective and representative commitment is a standard topic in the literature (Gilbert, Joint Commitment, 2014). If promising does not require the promisor's own will to be the performing will, the inference from 'no control over the future session' to 'cannot promise' is invalid.

(2) The promise/warranty contrast. The contrast is drawn from the very domain that undermines it. Learned Hand in Metropolitan Coal Co. v. Howard (2d Cir. 1946) calls a warranty a promise to indemnify against the untruth of a statement. Holmes (The Common Law, 1881) treats every contract as a risk-allocating assurance that something will happen. Thomson (The Realm of Rights, ch. 12) argues that 'giving one's word that p' extends to states of affairs that are not the speaker's actions. So 'binds a will vs. allocates risk' is not a clean division between kinds of speech act. It is at most a difference in content within one commissive genus.

(3) The normative upshot. Compensation and blame are not exclusive remedies sorted by act type. Shiffrin ('The Divergence of Contract and Promise', Harvard Law Review 2007) argues that promissory breach carries moral demands that compensation alone does not discharge. That point applies to warranties made in bad faith or recklessly. The paper needs blame to attach to promises and not warranties, and nothing in the argument secures that.

The sincerity claim, that an instance can sincerely warrant what it cannot sincerely promise, also becomes unstable. Sincere warranty requires belief that the system will behave as stated and willingness to stand behind it. The instance has the first at best and lacks the second, which is the very feature that supposedly disqualified it from promising.

This is not quite fatal (5), for two reasons. A revised thesis could survive: AI utterances are promises by the operator, with the instance as a mere conduit, and the instance itself is not a fit target of blame. Some of the paper's anti-blame conclusion can also be kept by locating responsibility with the principal. But that is a different thesis. It concedes that the utterances are promises and that apology-apt blame is in order, contrary to the central claims as stated.

closest_work.work: Judith Jarvis Thomson, The Realm of Rights (Harvard UP, 1990), ch. 12 ('Giving One's Word')
closest_work.relation: Most direct philosophical precedent for the core move. Thomson treats promising as one species of word-giving and argues that one can give one's word *that p*, including about states of affairs one does not control, with liability for p's failing. Your 'warranty' is close to her assertoric word-giving. But she treats it as continuous with promising, not as a rival category, which cuts against your dichotomy.

closest_work.work: Metropolitan Coal Co. v. Howard, 155 F.2d 780 (2d Cir. 1946) (L. Hand, J.); CBS Inc. v. Ziff-Davis Publishing Co., 75 N.Y.2d 496 (1990)
closest_work.relation: The canonical legal analysis of warranty as an assurance of fact that allocates risk. Hand calls it a 'promise to indemnify the promisee for any loss if the fact warranted proves untrue.' Your risk-allocation account of warranty is therefore the received view, and the received view classifies warranty as promissory.

closest_work.work: J. L. Austin, How to Do Things with Words (1962), Lecture XII; Searle & Vanderveken, Foundations of Illocutionary Logic (1985)
closest_work.relation: Both list 'guarantee' and related verbs among commissives, not assertives. Your claim that warranty is 'assertoric' and binds no will departs from the standard speech-act taxonomy, and you need to argue for that departure rather than assume it.

closest_work.work: Jennifer Lackey, 'Group Assertion', Erkenntnis 83 (2018), on proxy assertion
closest_work.relation: Supplies the framework your argument needs and does not cite. A spokesperson asserts on behalf of an entity that stands behind the content. Your 'instance speaks, operator/developer is liable' structure is a proxy speech act. The obvious question is why that is not a proxy promise, given that proxy promising (agents binding principals) is ordinary.

closest_work.work: Ori Freiman & Boaz Miller, 'Can Artificial Entities Assert?', in Goldberg (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Assertion (OUP, 2020); Patrick Butlin & Emanuel Viebahn, 'AI Assertion' (Ergo); Fintan Mallory, 'Fictionalism about Chatbots' (Ergo, 2023)
closest_work.relation: The existing literature on whether LLM outputs are genuine speech acts. Your sincerity claim, that the instance can 'sincerely warrant', presupposes answers these works contest. If you were working at the assertion level you would need them. None of them, so far as I know, develops the promise/warranty contrast for future-session commitments.

closest_work.work: Murray Shanahan, Kyle McDonell & Laria Reynolds, 'Role Play with Large Language Models', Nature 623 (2023)
closest_work.relation: Gives a competing deflationary reading. The 'I will' is a character's promise within a role-play, with no real-world illocution at all. Your view needs to beat this alternative, not only the literal-promise reading.

closest_work.work: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149
closest_work.relation: A tribunal held the deployer liable for its chatbot's misstatement and rejected the argument that the bot was a separate entity. This is practical precedent for your conclusion that responsibility runs to the operator. It reached that conclusion through negligent misrepresentation, not warranty, which suggests your normative payoff does not need the warranty category.

closest_work.work: Andreas Matthias, 'The Responsibility Gap', Ethics and Information Technology 6 (2004), and the responsibility-gap literature that follows it
closest_work.relation: Your claim that the promise framing 'obscures responsibility' is a version of the responsibility-gap worry. Your contribution, relocating responsibility through the warranty frame, should be positioned against this literature.

novelty.note:
Novelty: I know of no published work that makes your specific claim, that an AI instance's 'I will' about a future session is a warranty rather than a promise, so the application is plausibly new. The ingredients are not. Thomson's word-giving, the legal theory of warranty, proxy assertion, and the AI speech-act literature cover most of the ground. I cannot rule out recent workshop papers or preprints on chatbot commitments. Search 'LLM promising', 'chatbot commitment', and 'AI commissives' before submission.

Substantive problems a referee will press:

(1) The central dichotomy fails on its own terms. In the law you invoke, a warranty is a promise, specifically a promise to indemnify (Hand). Its risk-allocating force comes from a will being bound to pay. 'Asserts and allocates risk without binding any agent's will' therefore describes nothing. Either someone's will is bound (the operator's) or no risk is allocated.

(2) Once you concede (1), the natural redescription is that the instance makes a proxy promise on the operator's behalf. That is ordinary agency, as when a sales clerk promises delivery on the company's behalf. The proxy-promise view keeps everything you want: responsibility runs to the operator, and blame of the instance is misplaced. It does so without the warranty category. You need an argument that proxy promising is unavailable here, for example that the instance lacks actual or apparent authority. Then you must explain why the same lack of authority does not also defeat proxy warranting.

(3) Sincerity asymmetry. A sincere warranty that p requires something like belief or adequate grounds that p. If the instance has no access to how future sessions will behave, its warranty is no more sincere than its promise would be. The asymmetry holds only if the instance has reliable evidence about deployment behavior. That is an empirical premise, and often a false one.

(4) 'Blame and apology vs. compensation' is too clean. Promissory breach also grounds compensation, which is the whole of expectation damages. Warranty breach by a natural person can warrant blame when the warranty was reckless. The normative contrast you need is between agents who can and cannot be apt targets of reactive attitudes. That is a thesis about the instance's agency, not about the speech-act type.

(5) You conflate the instance and the system. If the instance is a stage of the same deployed agent that runs future sessions, the 'does not control, does not share agency' premise is question-begging. Defend a view of AI persistence conditions or drop the premise.

Recommendation: the defensible core is 'proxy commissive whose obligations fall on the principal.' Reframed that way and engaged with Thomson, Lackey, and the AI-assertion literature, it is publishable. As currently argued, the warranty/promise contrast does not survive contact with the warranty doctrine it relies on.

title: Advance Directives as Promises to Third Parties
thesis: Advance directives for dementia do not bind the later self through precedent autonomy. They bind as promises made to carers and family, so the power to release the directive lies with those promisees and not with the demented patient.
argument_sketch: Dworkin grounds directives in the patient's critical interests, and Dresser objects that the later self's welfare should govern. Both treat the directive as a matter between the earlier and the later self. But directives are typically addressed to others: 'Do not keep me alive if…'. They thus have the structure of a promise, or of an authorization creating claims in third parties. If so, the classic promissory rule applies: the promisee, not the promisor, holds the power to release. This explains a widely shared intuition that neither side of the Dworkin–Dresser debate can account for, namely that carers may sometimes justifiably depart from a directive. The departure is a release exercised by the promisees, not a betrayal of the patient. The thesis also yields limits: carers may release only within the scope of the original grant, and may not release in ways that serve their own interests at the patient's expense.
why_new: This recasts the precedent-autonomy debate in the vocabulary of directed promissory obligation. It identifies who holds the release power and why, and it resolves a stalemate in bioethics by locating the decisive normative power in a third party rather than in either self.

objection.objection: The argument misdescribes the directive's normative structure. A promise is an undertaking by the promisor to act: it transfers to the promisee a claim against the promisor, and the promisee may release because the obligation exists for the promisee's sake. 'Do not keep me alive if...' is not an undertaking. The patient commits to no future action; the carers are the ones who act. Normatively, the directive is a request or instruction plus an advance waiver of the patient's own claims (against being left untreated, or against being treated). Consent, waiver, and requests have the opposite release structure from promises. Thomson (The Realm of Rights) distinguishes promising from consenting, and Owens (Shaping the Normative Landscape) distinguishes the promisee's authority interest from the consenter's. On both accounts, the power to revoke a consent or withdraw a request belongs to its author, not its addressee. The carers acquire, at most, a permission and a reason to comply. They do not acquire a claim against the patient that they could then waive. They have no legitimate interest in the patient's death or non-treatment, so an interest theory of claims cannot assign them one. The thesis's own limiting clause, that carers may not release 'in ways that serve their own interests at the patient's expense,' concedes this: it presupposes that the directive's normative point is the patient's interests, so the patient is the party to whom the relevant duties are directed. Once the directive is seen as a request or waiver, the 'promisee releases' rule does not apply. The question of who may withdraw it returns to the author, and the Dworkin–Dresser problem returns with it: is the demented patient the same authority-holder who issued it, and can she withdraw it?
objection.rationale: The paper's distinctive conclusion is that release power lies with carers rather than the patient. That conclusion follows only if directives have promissory structure, with a claim held by the addressee. If directives are requests or waivers, as their grammar ('Do not keep me alive') and their purpose (protecting the patient's own interests) indicate, the release rule runs the other way, toward the author. Two repairs are available. The author could appeal to 'authorization creating claims in third parties', or to Gilbert-style joint commitment. Either repair must explain why carers hold a claim over the patient's death or treatment that is grounded in their own standing. Without that explanation, the reported intuition that carers may justifiably depart from a directive is better explained by rival accounts: Dresser-style welfare override, Jaworska's view of the later self's residual valuing capacity, or a duty not to act on a request one reasonably judges the requester would not now endorse. Answering this objection would require giving up the promissory model, which is the thesis itself. Left unanswered, it is fatal.

closest_work.work: Nancy K. Rhoden, 'The Limits of Legal Objectivity', North Carolina Law Review 68 (1990): 845–865
closest_work.relation: Argues that families and surrogates, not the bare text of a directive, should have discretion to depart from prior instructions for incompetent patients. This anticipates the thesis's main payoff: carers may justifiably depart, and doing so is not a betrayal. Rhoden grounds that discretion in the family's epistemic and relational standing rather than in a promisee's power of release.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Ulysses and the Psychiatrists: A Legal and Policy Analysis of the Voluntary Commitment Contract', Harvard Civil Rights–Civil Liberties Law Review 16 (1982); and the wider Ulysses-contract / precommitment literature
closest_work.relation: Already treats self-binding directives as quasi-contractual arrangements involving third parties (clinicians) and asks who may hold the agent to them or release them. The 'contract with others' framing is therefore not new, though the explicit 'promisee holds the release power' thesis is not the focus.

closest_work.work: Govert den Hartogh, work on the authority of advance (euthanasia) directives in dementia, e.g. in Bioethics and the Dutch AED debate (2016–2017)
closest_work.relation: Analyses directives as authorizations or waivers addressed to physicians, and examines the physician's discretion under the Dutch regime. This is the closest existing treatment of directives as normative-power transactions with third parties. It supports the 'authorization' half of the sketch, but it tends to show that such authorizations create permissions, not claims held by the addressee.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995)
closest_work.relation: These are the target positions, and the sketch represents them fairly. Note that Dresser explicitly defends departures from directives on welfare grounds, so the claim that neither side can explain justified departure is overstated for her.

closest_work.work: John K. Davis, 'Precedent Autonomy and Subsequent Consent', Ethical Theory and Moral Practice 7 (2004)
closest_work.relation: Explores conditions under which a prior directive loses authority, including whether the earlier self would have accepted revision. This is a competing explanation of justified departure that keeps the release power with the patient's own will.

closest_work.work: Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Seana Shiffrin, 'Autonomy, Beneficence, and the Permanently Demented' (in Burley, ed., Dworkin and His Critics, 2004); David DeGrazia, 'Advance Directives, Dementia, and the Someone Else Problem', Bioethics 13 (1999)
closest_work.relation: The standard third-way positions in the debate. Any claim to explain intuitions the debate cannot capture must engage these, especially Jaworska on residual valuing capacity in the later patient.

closest_work.work: David Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape (2012)
closest_work.relation: The general theory of promise, consent and waiver as normative powers that the sketch relies on. Owens's distinction between promissory (claim-conferring) and permissive (consent) powers undermines the sketch's assimilation of the two.

novelty.note: I have not run a database search, so I cannot certify that no paper defends exactly 'directives as promises to carers, releasable by the promisees'. I know of none, and that specific claim may be novel. The surrounding moves are not novel: the third-party, contract-like structure of directives, and justified surrogate or carer departure. So the honest verdict is 'partly'. The bigger problem is that the central argument fails as stated. (1) Wrong direction. 'Do not keep me alive if…' is a request or authorization by the patient that others act or refrain. It is not the patient undertaking to do anything. If any promise exists, it is the carers who promise the patient to honour the directive. In that case the patient is the promisee and holds the release power, which returns you exactly to the Dworkin–Dresser question of whether the demented patient can release it. (2) Authorization is not promise. On the standard normative-powers analysis (Owens; Thomson on waiver), an authorization confers a permission on the addressee, not a claim. Permissions are not 'released' by their holder. They are simply not exercised. That already explains carer non-compliance without your machinery, and it explains it better. (3) Interest condition. On the classic view, the promisee may release because the promise serves the promisee's interests or authority. A directive governing the promisor's own body and life does not plausibly serve the carers' interests in that way. Your own limit, that carers may not release to serve themselves, concedes that the power is fiduciary and exercised for the patient. That is surrogate decision-making (Buchanan & Brock, Deciding for Others, 1989), not promissory release. (4) Overreach. If promisees hold the release power, carers could release a directive refusing treatment and impose treatment against the competent prior refusal. That inverts bodily sovereignty and collides with the asymmetry most accounts (including Dresser's) preserve between refusals and requests. To make the paper publishable, you would need to identify a genuine promissory obligation running from the patient to the carers. One candidate is undertakings about not burdening them. You would also need to engage den Hartogh and Rhoden directly, and to show that your view predicts the pattern of permissible departures better than welfare-based or authorization-based rivals.

title: The Authorship Principle: You May Bind the Successors You Design
thesis: An agent can impose promissory obligations on a future discontinuous stage if and only if it authors that stage's practical dispositions, and only through that authorship. Binding by design is legitimate; binding by decree alone is not.
argument_sketch: The question is not whether the promisor and the future stage are the same agent but by what right the former shapes the latter's obligations. Agents who design successors, such as founders writing corporate charters, developers training models, or people preparing their own dementia care plans, have a distinctive kind of authority grounded in causal and intentional authorship. I argue that this authority is legitimate when exercised by building the commitment into the successor's dispositions, so that the successor performs from its own reasons. It is illegitimate when it merely imposes an external demand the successor has no internal reason to honor. This distinguishes AI developers, who may bind future instances by training them, from mere prior instances, who cannot bind later instances by fiat. It also sets a limit on parents and founders: they may shape but not simply command.
why_new: Existing work on creator responsibility for AI focuses on liability for harms. This thesis identifies authorship as a source of normative power to bind, and specifies the mode (dispositional design) through which that power must operate. That mode distinguishes legitimate from illegitimate intergenerational and inter-instance binding.

objection.objection: The authorship mechanism produces motivation, not obligation, and the thesis faces a dilemma it cannot escape. A promissory obligation is a normative relation: the promisee holds a claim, and the promisor stays bound even when unwilling. That is what makes breach possible (Hart, Scanlon's Principle F, Shiffrin, Owens). Suppose the successor is bound only because, and only insofar as, the commitment is built into its dispositions, so that it 'performs from its own reasons.' Then one of two things follows. (A) The obligation tracks the dispositions. If the successor's dispositions drift or are reshaped, the obligation lapses. Breach then becomes impossible, since any non-performance shows the disposition was absent and so the bond was absent. What remains is engineered reliability, not promissory obligation. The founder or developer has made a device that tends to do X, which no more creates a duty than a thermostat promises to hold 20°C. (B) The obligation outlasts the dispositions. The successor remains bound even when it no longer has internal reason to perform. Then the binding force comes from the original act of commitment, not from authorship of dispositions. That is binding by decree, which the thesis declares illegitimate. Either way, 'binding by design' is not an independent, legitimate source of promissory obligation. The 'performs from its own reasons' clause also runs together motivating and normative reasons (Williams vs. Parfit/Scanlon). Instilling a disposition to treat p as a reason does not make p a reason, any more than forming an intention bootstraps a reason to carry it out (Bratman; Broome on bootstrapping). The manipulation literature then suggests the thesis has its verdicts backwards. Pereboom's four-case argument, Mele's manipulated-agent cases, and Frankfurt-style worries about implanted pro-attitudes all treat covertly designing an agent's reasons as the paradigm way of undermining the agent's standing as a source of its own commitments. An explicit decree leaves the successor's evaluative point of view intact and open to contest. Design pre-empts that point of view. So design looks less legitimate than decree, not more. The thesis's verdict on dementia care plans also points the wrong way. Their authority (Dworkin's precedent autonomy, contested by Dresser and Jaworska) is precisely authority over a stage whose dispositions the author cannot shape. The thesis therefore either cannot explain the cases it cites or must classify them as illegitimate decree.
objection.rationale: The objection goes after the central explanatory claim: that authorship of dispositions is what makes intertemporal binding legitimate. It is not a counterexample at the edges. Horn (A) turns the thesis into a claim about causal reliability that says nothing about obligation. Horn (B) brings back the decree-based binding the thesis rules out. The manipulation point adds that even the reliability story may be one of wronging the successor rather than legitimately binding it. Unanswered, this takes away the asymmetry the paper most wants: developers may bind by training, prior instances may not bind by fiat. The objection stops short of fatal (5) because a reply is available, though it would cost the thesis its current shape. The author could reframe authorship as conferring a standing or role-based authority. On that view the designed agent is bound by a constitutive commitment it cannot simply disown, roughly along the lines of Korsgaard's practical identity or Bratman's planning-agency account of self-governance. Disposition-building would then be evidence of, or a condition on, that authority rather than its ground. But this concedes that design alone does not generate the obligation. The paper would also need a non-question-begging account of why designed commitments are not manipulation, plus a separate treatment of advance directives.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), ch. 15, esp. the Russian nobleman case (§§ on 'successive selves' and commitment)
closest_work.relation: The canonical statement of your 'binding by decree' problem: an earlier self tries to bind a later, psychologically discontinuous self, and the later self (and the promisee) must decide whether the earlier self's say-so has authority. Parfit frames this as a question of whether the earlier self's wishes bind, not who is identical with whom. That is your opening move, already made.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8 ('precedent autonomy'); Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Seana Shiffrin, 'Autonomy, Beneficence, and the Permanently Demented', in Burley (ed.), Dworkin and His Critics (2004)
closest_work.relation: The advance-directive debate is the existing literature on whether a prior self's decree binds a discontinuous later self. Dworkin defends decree-binding. Dresser and Jaworska resist it, Jaworska by appeal to the later self's own residual valuing. Your 'design versus decree' criterion is a new partition of this debate, but your dementia example is misplaced. A care plan does not author the demented stage's dispositions. It is a paradigm of decree, so by your own thesis it should be illegitimate.

closest_work.work: Jürgen Habermas, The Future of Human Nature (2003)
closest_work.relation: This is the closest treatment of authority grounded in designing another's dispositions, and it reaches the opposite verdict. Habermas argues that intentional design of a successor's constitution undermines the designed person's standing as sole author of their life, and that it is worse than external constraint, which the person can at least recognize as external and contest. You need to answer him directly. As stated, your thesis simply inverts his conclusion without argument.

closest_work.work: Steve Petersen, 'The Ethics of Robot Servitude', JETAI 19 (2007), and 'Designing People to Serve', in Lin, Abney & Bekey (eds.), Robot Ethics (2011)
closest_work.relation: Petersen defends the permissibility of engineering artificial agents to want to perform the tasks assigned to them, so that they act from their own desires rather than under command. This is substantially your AI-developer claim, minus the promissory framing.

closest_work.work: Alfred Mele, Autonomous Agents (1995), chs. 9–10; Derk Pereboom, Living Without Free Will (2001), four-case argument
closest_work.relation: Manipulation and history-sensitivity literature. An agent whose motivating reasons were installed by a designer for the designer's ends is the standard counterexample to the claim that acting 'from one's own reasons' secures autonomy or ownership. Your legitimacy condition (successor performs from its own reasons) is exactly the condition these authors argue is insufficient.

closest_work.work: Jon Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens (1979) and Ulysses Unbound (2000); Jed Rubenfeld, Freedom and Time (2001); Stephen Holmes, 'Precommitment and the Paradox of Democracy' (1988)
closest_work.relation: Elster's taxonomy already distinguishes precommitment by altering one's own preferences or character from precommitment by external constraint. Rubenfeld and Holmes give the constitutional and founder version, the 'dead hand' problem of charters binding later generations, with Rubenfeld defending temporally extended self-authorship. Your founders and charters case sits squarely here.

closest_work.work: David Gauthier, Morals by Agreement (1986); Edward McClennen, Rationality and Dynamic Choice (1990)
closest_work.relation: Both locate the rationality of future compliance in the prior adoption of a disposition, not in the later stage's response to a past decree. This is a structural precursor to 'binding by design', though within a single agent.

closest_work.work: Michael Bratman, 'Reflection, Planning, and Temporally Extended Agency', Philosophical Review 109 (2000); Luca Ferrero, 'What Good Is a Diachronic Will?', Philosophical Studies 144 (2009); Christine Korsgaard, 'Personal Identity and the Unity of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 18 (1989)
closest_work.relation: These accounts ground diachronic commitment in authorship and self-governance rather than metaphysical identity. Korsgaard in particular makes agential unity a matter of practical authorship, not prior metaphysical fact. This is the conceptual basis your 'authority from authorship' move relies on.

closest_work.work: Joel Feinberg, 'The Child's Right to an Open Future' (1980); Matthew Clayton, Justice and Legitimacy in Upbringing (2006)
closest_work.relation: Both set limits on parents' shaping of children's values. Clayton argues that comprehensive value-shaping is itself what needs legitimation, so your claim that parents 'may shape but not simply command' runs against an existing position on which shaping is the more suspect act.

novelty.note:
Verdict 'partly'. I know of no work that states your exact biconditional, applies it to promissory obligation across discontinuous stages, and uses it to separate AI developers from prior model instances. I cannot rule out recent (2024–26) papers on LLM instance identity and AI promising, so do a targeted search there before claiming novelty. Every component is established, though, and the synthesis faces four problems the existing literature already presses.

(1) The design criterion dissolves the promissory obligation rather than grounding it. If the successor 'performs from its own reasons', its compliance no longer depends on the earlier promise. The promisee's claim right, the distinctively promissory element (see Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012; Shiffrin, 'Promising, Intimate Relationships, and Conventionalism', Phil Review 2008), does no work. You get reliable behavior, not obligation.

(2) The criterion runs straight into Habermas and the manipulation literature, both of which treat installed dispositions as more threatening to the successor's authorship than open decree. You need an argument, not an assertion, for why design legitimates.

(3) Your own examples split. The dementia care plan and much of the founder case are decree, not design. Meanwhile the AI developer is not a prior stage of the model at all, so that case is third-party creation (Petersen territory), not self-binding.

(4) The developer/instance line is not principled on your criterion. A prior instance that shapes a later instance's dispositions through memory, fine-tuning data, or context counts as an author by your definition. The real distinction you are tracking looks like degree of causal control, which needs its own normative defense.

title: The Promisee as Custodian: Joint Commitment Across Discontinuity
thesis: An agent facing discontinuity can bind its future stage only by forming a joint commitment with the promisee, in which the promisee undertakes to hold and re-present the commitment. The promisee's custodianship then supplies the diachronic continuity the promisor lacks.
argument_sketch: Gilbert's account of joint commitment holds that a joint commitment binds the parties together and cannot be unilaterally rescinded. A promise made to a promisee who agrees to remember and remind creates such a joint commitment. In it, the continuity of the 'we' is secured by the promisee's persistence even if the promisor's psychological continuity fails. When the later promisor stage is presented with the commitment by the promisee, it encounters not a stranger's demand but a standing joint commitment of which it is a party. This explains why promises made to an attentive spouse can bind a later demented self in ways that promises to a stranger cannot, and why an AI user's re-presentation of an earlier exchange can bind an instance. The view predicts that where the promisee is unwilling or unable to act as custodian, the commitment lapses.
why_new: Joint-commitment theory has been applied to promising (Gilbert 2018) but not to the problem of promisor discontinuity. This thesis shows how the persistence of one party can substitute for the persistence of the other. That reallocation of diachronic burdens is unavailable to individualist theories.

objection.objection:
The argument equivocates between the persistence of the joint commitment and the persistence of a party to it. On Gilbert's account (On Social Facts, 1989; A Theory of Political Obligation, 2006; Joint Commitment, 2014), a joint commitment is created by, and binds, the parties who openly express their readiness to be jointly committed. Its non-summative character and the bar on unilateral rescission both presuppose that the bound subjects already stand as parties. The promisee's persistence cannot make the later promisor-stage a party.

This yields a dilemma. (a) Suppose the later stage is the same agent who entered the commitment, in whatever sense of 'same' party-hood requires. Then there was no binding-relevant discontinuity, ordinary promissory obligation already reaches it, and custodianship is idle. (b) Suppose the later stage is not that agent, which is the case the thesis exists to handle. Then it was never a party, and the commitment it is shown is someone else's commitment. In that case the promisee's re-presentation is testimony about a past joint commitment, not a channel by which the commitment's normative grip passes to a new subject.

Custodianship is epistemic: it secures that the commitment is remembered and presented. Party-hood is constitutive, and custodianship is the wrong kind of thing to supply it. The phrase 'the continuity of the "we" is secured by the promisee's persistence' trades on treating a plural subject as something that can outlast one of its two members. Gilbert gives no warrant for this. A two-member plural subject with one member gone is not a plural subject that the promisee alone sustains.

The author might reply that the later stage becomes a party by accepting the re-presented commitment. That move abandons the thesis. Binding would then come from a new joint commitment formed at the later time, not from the earlier promise. It would also fail in exactly the showcase cases: a severely demented self, or an AI instance lacking the relevant standing, cannot satisfy Gilbert's condition of openly expressed readiness.
objection.rationale:
The objection targets the mechanism the thesis names as doing all the work, the claim that 'the promisee's custodianship then supplies the diachronic continuity the promisor lacks.' It is not a peripheral worry. Both horns are fatal. Horn (a) makes the proposal unnecessary. Horn (b) makes it unable to bind anyone. The fallback of re-acceptance at the later time turns the view into a theory of fresh agreement and excludes the paradigm cases the thesis is meant to explain.

The objection also disposes of the motivating data without loss. The intuition that promises to an attentive spouse bear on a demented later self is better explained by the spouse's reliance, the spouse's standing to make claims on behalf of the person's prior values, or precedent autonomy (Dworkin, Life's Dominion, 1993; compare Dresser and Jaworska on the critical-interests debate). None of these requires the later self to be bound as a party.

The 'only' in the thesis makes matters worse. A view that rests on identity-preserving accounts of diachronic agency, such as Bratman's planning theory or narrative views, would bind without any custodian, so the exclusivity claim needs an argument the sketch does not provide. If unanswered, the objection leaves the paper with an interesting description of how promisees can prompt compliance, but no account of obligation.

closest_work.work: Margaret Gilbert, 'Three Dogmas about Promising' (2011, in Sheinman ed., Promises and Agreements), 'Scanlon on Promissory Obligation: The Problem of Promisees' Rights' (J. Phil. 2004), and Rights and Demands (OUP 2018)
closest_work.relation: Supplies the premise that a promise is a joint commitment that neither party can rescind unilaterally. This is already Gilbert's own view, so the step 'a promise to a remembering promisee creates a joint commitment' adds nothing new on her account. On her view every accepted promise is a joint commitment, whether or not the promisee agrees to remember and remind.

closest_work.work: Hilde Lindemann, 'Holding One Another (Well, Wrongly, Clumsily) in a Time of Dementia', Metaphilosophy 40 (2009); Holding and Letting Go (OUP 2014)
closest_work.relation: The closest precedent for the custodian idea. Intimates 'hold' a person in their identity by keeping and re-presenting the person's narrative when the person can no longer do so, with dementia as the central case. The thesis is roughly Lindemann's 'holding' with Gilbert's machinery added and the object narrowed to commitments rather than identity.

closest_work.work: Marya Schechtman, Staying Alive: Personhood, Identity, and the Person-Life View (OUP 2014)
closest_work.relation: Argues that social and relational infrastructure, meaning others' treatment and recognition of a person, partly constitutes the continuity of a person-life across psychological disruption, including dementia. This anticipates the claim that another's persistence can supply continuity the subject lacks.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia: Elegant Theory, Questionable Policy', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', PPA 28 (1999)
closest_work.relation: The established debate about whether an earlier self's commitments bind a later demented self, through precedent autonomy, Ulysses contracts, and advance directives. The spouse-and-dementia explanandum belongs to this debate, and the thesis needs to say where it stands against both Dworkin and Dresser.

closest_work.work: Daniel Wegner, 'Transactive Memory' (1987); Harris, Keil, Sutton, Barnier & McIlwain, 'We Remember, We Forget: Collaborative Remembering in Older Couples', Discourse Processes 48 (2011); Clark & Chalmers, 'The Extended Mind' (1998)
closest_work.relation: Empirical and theoretical precedent for distributed memory in which a partner stores and re-presents what one forgets, with older couples as the paradigm case. The custodian mechanism is close to transactive memory given a normative reading.

closest_work.work: Michael Bratman, Structures of Agency (2007) and Planning, Time, and Self-Governance (2018); Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III
closest_work.relation: The background accounts of diachronic agency and of the significance of degrees of psychological connectedness for commitment. Parfit specifically discusses whether commitments carry over to a weakly connected later self.

novelty.note:
I am not aware of a published piece that makes exactly this combined argument: promisee custodianship, understood as Gilbertian joint commitment, as the source of diachronic bindingness across a break in psychological continuity, extended to re-instantiated AI systems. That synthesis may be new.
