Each component, however, is already in the literature (Gilbert on promise as joint commitment; Lindemann and Schechtman on others holding a person's continuity through dementia; transactive memory), and the paper must engage Lindemann in particular or a referee will treat it as unacknowledged. I cannot rule out recent work on AI agents and commitment that I have not seen, so a targeted search of 2023–2026 work on LLM agency and promising is warranted.

The argument also has a serious structural problem: the key move begs the question. The later stage 'encounters a standing joint commitment of which it is a party' only if it is the same party, or the party's successor, who entered it. That is exactly what discontinuity puts in doubt. The promisee's persistence secures the persistence of one relatum. It does not secure the identity of the other, and a joint commitment with a party who no longer exists is not thereby a commitment held by whoever is presented with it. Gilbert's no-unilateral-rescission principle governs parties. It cannot be used to make someone a party.

Second, the lapse prediction conflicts with Gilbert's own account. Joint commitments do not lapse because a party forgets them. If custodianship is necessary for continued bindingness, the view has departed from Gilbert and needs an independent account of why re-presentation is constitutive rather than merely evidential.

Third, the custodian is also the holder of the release power. The view therefore gives the promisee unilateral control over whether the commitment survives, simply by declining to re-present it. This collapses the joint structure the argument relies on and threatens to make bindingness depend on the promisee's will.

Fourth, the dementia asymmetry (spouse versus stranger) may be better explained by relational and evidential factors, such as trust, shared history, and access to the person's prior values, than by a difference in normative structure. The author should show why the deflationary explanation fails.

Finally, the AI case needs separate argument. It is unclear that an instance has the standing to enter a Gilbertian joint commitment at all, and a user's re-presentation of a transcript is compatible with the instance treating it as testimony about a different agent.

title: Discontinuity as a Crucial Test: Authority Theories Beat Expectation Theories
thesis: Promises across psychological discontinuity are a crucial test case that discriminates between theories of promissory obligation. Expectation-based theories (Scanlon's Principle F) cannot explain why such promises bind, and authority-based theories (Owens) can.
argument_sketch: On expectation views, the duty is owed by whoever voluntarily and intentionally led the promisee to expect performance. In discontinuity cases, that agent no longer exists at performance time, so the theory can locate the wrong only in the earlier stage's act of inducing expectation. That collapses promissory obligation into a duty of care in assertion. Authority views ground the obligation in the promisee's interest in having authority over the promisor's conduct. That authority is a property of the promisee's normative position, which persists, and can therefore attach to whatever agent occupies the promised role. I show that the authority view correctly predicts that promisees retain claims against corporate successors and AI deployments. The expectation view predicts only claims against past agents, which are often unreachable. The discontinuity cases are thus evidence for the authority view, which has struggled to find decisive support.
why_new: Debates between Scanlonian and Owensian theories have been conducted using ordinary cases in which both theories agree. This thesis identifies a class of cases in which they diverge in their predictions and argues that intuitive verdicts favor one side, providing new evidence in a long-running dispute.

objection.objection: The discontinuity cases do not discriminate between the two theories, because the explanatory work is done by a succession principle that is independent of both and equally available to each. On Owens's view (Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012, chs. 4-6), the promisee's authority interest is an interest in having a bipolar normative relation to the very agent who exercised the normative power of promising. The promisor's act of will creates the authority, and the authority is over that promisor's conduct. Authority is therefore two-place, not a free-floating property of the promisee's position. If the promisor ceases to exist, the authority loses its second relatum exactly as Scanlon's directed duty loses its bearer. The argument's key move, that authority 'can attach to whatever agent occupies the promised role,' is not part of the authority view. It is an added principle of role-based transmission of obligation, akin to the legal assumption of liabilities by corporate successors. That principle is not derived from the promisee's interest in authority. It also cuts against Owens's own emphasis that promissory authority is grounded in, and limited by, the promisor's voluntary transfer (Thompson, 'What Is It to Wrong Someone?', 2004, and Darwall, The Second-Person Standpoint, 2006, on the bipolarity of directed obligation). Once such a principle is on the table, the expectation theorist can adopt it without strain. Scanlon's Principle F (What We Owe to Each Other, 1998, ch. 7) is a principle requiring performance, not merely care in assertion, and Scanlon distinguishes it explicitly from Principles M and D. So the charge that the view 'collapses promissory obligation into a duty of care in assertion' misdescribes it. An F-theorist can say that the duty to perform is borne by whoever succeeds to the promisor's practical standing, by the same transmission rule. The asymmetry the thesis needs, that authority persists where expectation-based duties cannot, comes from a stipulation about one theory's relata, not from the theories themselves. The cases also rest on contested data. Whether promisees have genuinely promissory claims against corporate successors and AI deployments, as opposed to contractual, restitutionary, or reliance-based claims, is exactly what is in dispute. Parfit's discussion of commitments across psychological change (Reasons and Persons, 1984, §§ 102-106) suggests the intuitions are unstable.
objection.rationale: The thesis is specifically that discontinuity cases are a test that discriminates between the views and favors authority. If role-attachment is an independent succession principle that either theory can adopt, or that neither can justify from its own resources, the cases discriminate nothing. They would instead test a theory of how obligations pass between agents, and the claimed new evidence for Owens disappears. The misreading of Principle F compounds the problem by removing the supposed weakness of the expectation view. The author could try to show that authority, unlike expectation, has an internal, non-ad hoc reason to attach to roles, for instance by modeling promissory authority on office-based authority. But that would be a different and much more ambitious paper, and it would be in tension with Owens's own voluntarist grounding. Unanswered, the objection defeats the central claim rather than merely weakening it.

closest_work.work: David Owens, 'A Simple Theory of Promising', Philosophical Review 115 (2006); and Shaping the Normative Landscape (OUP 2012), chs. 4–6
closest_work.relation: Source of the authority-interest view and of the main anti-expectation arguments, though not the discontinuity argument. Owens attacks Scanlon with cases where the promisee forms no expectation, does not rely, or would not be harmed (e.g. promises the promisee does not believe will be kept), and concludes that the obligation answers to an interest in authority rather than in assurance. The proposed paper reuses this explanatory contrast with a new diagnostic case. Note that Owens's authority is a bipolar relation to the particular promisor who exercised a normative power. Nothing in Owens makes it a property of the promisee's position that 'attaches to whatever agent occupies the promised role.' That extension belongs to the author and needs independent defense.

closest_work.work: T. M. Scanlon, 'Promises and Practices', Philosophy & Public Affairs 19 (1990); What We Owe to Each Other (1998), ch. 7
closest_work.relation: Target view. Directly relevant because Scanlon separates Principle F from Principles M (manipulation), D (due care), and L (loss prevention). F's distinctive content is that the promisor must perform, not merely take care in inducing expectations. The claim that the expectation view 'collapses promissory obligation into a duty of care in assertion' is therefore something Scanlon explicitly anticipated and rejected. The paper must show why discontinuity forces the collapse, not just assert it.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, 'Later Selves and Moral Principles' (in Montefiore ed., Philosophy and Personal Relations, 1973); Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III, esp. ch. 15 and the 'Russian nobleman' case (§ on earlier selves and commitments)
closest_work.relation: Closest precedent on promising across psychological discontinuity. Parfit argues that weakening psychological connectedness can weaken commitments made by an earlier self, and he discusses whether the later self is bound by, or may release, the earlier self's undertakings. He does not use the cases to adjudicate expectation vs. authority accounts, but the core phenomenon, and the worry that the obligation-bearer may 'no longer exist', are his.

closest_work.work: Seana Shiffrin, 'Promising, Intimate Relationships, and Conventionalism', Philosophical Review 117 (2008); 'The Divergence of Contract and Promise', Harvard Law Review 120 (2007)
closest_work.relation: Another prominent non-expectation account (relational, normative-power-based). It is a competitor the paper ignores. If discontinuity cases tell against Scanlon, they may support Shiffrin's or a generic normative-power view just as well as Owens's, so they would not discriminate in Owens's favor specifically.

closest_work.work: Margaret Gilbert, Rights and Demands (OUP 2018); 'Three Dogmas about Promising' (in Sheinman ed., Promises and Agreements, 2011)
closest_work.relation: Joint-commitment account on which promissory obligation attaches to a plural subject rather than to an individual's psychology. It already offers a non-expectation explanation of how commitments persist through changes in membership and constitution, the corporate-successor half of the argument. Gilbert is a rival explanation the paper must rule out.

closest_work.work: Christian List & Philip Pettit, Group Agency (OUP 2011); Kendy Hess, 'The Peculiar Unity of Corporate Agents' (in Orts & Smith eds., The Moral Responsibility of Firms, 2017)
closest_work.relation: Accounts of corporate agency on which corporations persist as agents through member turnover. These undercut the paper's corporate cases. If the corporation is the same agent, the expectation view simply locates the duty in that continuing agent, and the cases are not discontinuity cases at all.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995)
closest_work.relation: The 'precedent autonomy' and advance-directive debate already treats how far an earlier self's commitments bind across radical psychological change. This is the most developed applied literature on the phenomenon, and the paper should engage it.

closest_work.work: Allen Habib, 'Promises', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Kolodny & Wallace, 'Promises and Practices Revisited', Philosophy & Public Affairs 31 (2003)
closest_work.relation: Standard maps of the expectation/practice/normative-power dialectic. They show the expectation-vs-authority contest is well trodden. Novelty must lie wholly in the discontinuity test.

novelty.note:
Novelty: The pieces are all in print: Parfit on promises across discontinuity, Owens's authority interest versus Scanlon's Principle F, and Gilbert and List–Pettit on persisting collective commitments. I know of no published paper that uses discontinuity cases as a crucial experiment between Scanlon and Owens, or that extends the argument to AI deployments. I cannot rule out recent journal or working-paper literature, so I say 'partly', not 'novel'. The specific framing is probably publishable as new. The substantive claims face serious problems.

(1) Symmetry. If the promisor genuinely no longer exists, both views lose the duty-bearer. Owens's interest is in having authority over this promisor, who exercised the power. The paper gets successors bound only by adding a role-based transfer principle, and that principle does the real work. The same principle could be added to Scanlon: 'whoever occupies the role must not disappoint expectations induced by its prior occupant.' The cases then discriminate between role-based and individual-based accounts, not between expectation and authority.

(2) Misreading Scanlon. Principle F already requires performance, distinct from Principle D (due care). Scanlon can say the wrong is the continuing agent's non-performance where there is a continuing agent. Where there is none, he can say there is no promissory wrong, only the earlier act. That is arguably the correct verdict, and the paper assumes otherwise without argument.

(3) The corporate cases are not discontinuity cases on the leading theories of group agency. AI 'deployments' raise a prior question, whether the system was ever a promisor, that the paper skips.

(4) The intuitions are not clean. Successor liability in law is a policy-driven doctrine. Treating it as evidence about moral promissory obligation needs defense, especially since many people judge that a successor who never undertook anything is not bound, which is Parfit's verdict.

(5) Shiffrin and Gilbert are unaddressed rivals. Even granting the cases, they would not uniquely favor Owens.

Recommendation: Narrow the thesis to 'discontinuity cases pressure individual-psychological grounding of promissory obligation.' Engage Parfit, the precedent-autonomy literature, and Gilbert directly. Defend the role-transfer principle explicitly instead of attributing it to Owens.

title: Discontinuity Dissolves the Paradox of Self-Promising
thesis: The standard objection to promises to oneself, that the promisee can always release the promisor and so no binding occurs, fails when promisor and promisee are psychologically discontinuous stages. Discontinuous agents can therefore make genuinely binding self-promises in a way continuous agents cannot.
argument_sketch: Hobbes, and later Habib, argued that self-promises are empty because the person who is bound is also the person with power to release. When the earlier stage promises the later stage, however, and the two lack psychological continuity, they do not share the same will. The later stage holds the release power and the earlier stage holds the obligation, or vice versa, and these are not exercised by a single will. So the release objection loses its force. This yields a counterintuitive result: an agent anticipating dementia may make a promise to her future self, and that promise may bind her pre-dementia stage in a way an ordinary self-promise could not. It also clarifies what self-promising theorists like Rosati were reaching for.
why_new: Defenses of self-promising (Rosati, Habib) try to answer the release objection within a single continuous self. This thesis argues that the objection is decisive for continuous selves but inapplicable across discontinuity. It thereby relocates the conditions for genuine self-promising and links two literatures, self-promising and personal identity, that have developed separately.

objection.objection: The argument faces an identity dilemma and cannot keep both 'self' and 'binding.' Take the first horn. Suppose the earlier and later stages are psychologically discontinuous in the sense required to deny them a shared will, and identity is fixed by psychological continuity (Locke, Parfit 1984, Shoemaker). Then they are not the same person, and the 'self-promise' is an ordinary promise to another person who happens to share one's body, a Parfitian successor. That it binds is unsurprising and says nothing about self-promising. Take the second horn. Suppose identity is fixed by something else, say the animal (Olson 1997), so the stages count as one self. Then sameness of self is doing no work in the release objection. That objection, from Hobbes (Leviathan ch. 26, 'he that can bind can release') and Marcus Singer ('On Duties to Oneself,' Ethics 1959), was never about numerical identity. It was about whether the authority to waive the obligation and the bearer of the obligation coincide. Once the argument concedes they do not coincide, it has conceded that this is not the case the objection targets. In neither horn is there a distinctive class of genuinely binding self-promises. A further point shows that discontinuity is not doing the work even on its own terms. In the dementia case, what blocks release is that the promisee does not yet exist, or cannot exercise normative powers, during the window in which the earlier stage must perform. That temporal asymmetry holds equally for a fully continuous agent promising her future self. So the claimed contrast with continuous agents does not follow. A second problem compounds this. On authority-based accounts of promising (Owens 2012; Shiffrin 2008), a promisee who cannot accept, waive, or hold the promisor to account is no promisee. What remains in the dementia case is a resolution or vow, not a promise.
objection.rationale: This objection targets the conjunction the thesis needs: that the cases are self-promises and that they escape the release objection. It also shows the payoff ('in a way continuous agents cannot') does not follow, because temporal non-coexistence, not discontinuity, blocks release. It falls short of fatal only because the author could retreat to a weaker claim with a third route. On that route, 'self' is tracked by a relation such as narrative ownership or Parfitian 'what matters' in a degree that survives loss of strong connectedness, and release authority is tracked by a separate condition. That would need a worked-out account of how the two come apart, and the current sketch has none. The paper also has scholarly problems a referee would flag. First, Allen Habib ('Promises to the Self,' Canadian Journal of Philosophy 2009) defends the possibility of self-promises against the release objection rather than advancing it, so pairing him with Hobbes misreports the dialectic. Second, Rosati ('The Importance of Self-Promises,' 2011) grounds their value in the autonomy and self-trust of a continuous agent. Claiming she was 'reaching for' a discontinuity view needs textual support it currently lacks.

closest_work.work: Paul Schofield, Duty to Self: Moral, Political, and Legal Self-Relation (Oxford University Press, 2021)
closest_work.relation: Closest structural precedent. Schofield answers the release/paradox objection to duties owed to oneself by treating the agent's present and future selves as occupying distinct practical standpoints, so that one temporal self can stand in a directed, second-personal relation to another. Your core move is that temporally separated stages are not 'a single will' and so the release objection fails. That is a specific version of this strategy. It differs mainly in tying the distinctness to psychological discontinuity rather than to diachronic standpoint as such.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (Oxford, 1984), Part Three, incl. the Russian nobleman case and the discussion of obligations and commitments across reduced psychological connectedness
closest_work.relation: Supplies the metaphysical premise you rely on: diminished connectedness makes a later self relevantly like another person for purposes of commitment, desert, and obligation. The nobleman case is in effect a precommitment directed against a future, psychologically altered self, with a third party holding the release power. Your argument applies Parfitian reductionism to the release objection. Parfit already draws the general moral that commitments to and from a disconnected future self behave like commitments between different people.

closest_work.work: Daniel Muñoz, 'The Paradox of Duties to Oneself', Australasian Journal of Philosophy 98 (2020)
closest_work.relation: Recent focused treatment of the release objection (Kant MM 6:417; Singer 1959). It argues the objection fails for reasons that do not depend on splitting the self. That makes it a direct competitor: if Muñoz is right, discontinuity is not needed to defeat release, which undercuts your claim that only discontinuous agents can bind themselves.

closest_work.work: Marcus G. Singer, 'On Duties to Oneself', Ethics 69 (1959); Hobbes, Leviathan ch. 26 and De Cive 6.14
closest_work.relation: The canonical statements of the release objection. Hobbes's version concerns the sovereign's inability to be bound by civil law, since 'he that can bind can release'. It is not specifically about promising. Singer gives the modern formulation for duties to self. You should cite Singer and the Kantian paradox, not only Hobbes.

closest_work.work: Allen Habib, 'Promises to the Self', Canadian Journal of Philosophy 39 (2009)
closest_work.relation: Your sketch attributes the emptiness thesis to Habib. My recollection is that Habib defends the coherence of self-promises against the release worry rather than endorsing it. Please verify. If I am right, Habib is a rival defense of self-promising, not a proponent of the objection, and the framing of the paper needs correcting.

closest_work.work: Connie S. Rosati, 'The Importance of Self-Promising', in H. Sheinman (ed.), Promises and Agreements (OUP, 2011)
closest_work.relation: Defends self-promising as an exercise of autonomy and self-trust over time, with the later self figuring as the party to whom one answers. Your claim to 'clarify what Rosati was reaching for' has to engage the fact that her account depends on continuity of a self-governing agent. Splitting the agent into discontinuous parties arguably abandons her project rather than completing it.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8; Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report 25 (1995); Allen Buchanan, 'Advance Directives and the Personal Identity Problem', Philosophy & Public Affairs 17 (1988); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Philosophy & Public Affairs 28 (1999); Dresser, 'Ulysses and the Psychiatrists' (1982)
closest_work.relation: The dementia application belongs to the precedent-autonomy and Ulysses-contract literature. That literature already debates whether a pre-dementia 'then-self' can bind, or be bound with respect to, a discontinuous 'now-self', and whether discontinuity makes the later individual a distinct party. Framing this as promising, and the direction of obligation you describe (later to earlier), is less common, but the terrain is well trodden.

novelty.note:
The ingredients are not new. Defeating the release objection by distinguishing temporal selves appears in Schofield and, in germ, in Parfit. Discontinuity making a later individual a distinct moral party is Parfit, Buchanan, and Dresser. The dementia/precommitment case is the advance-directive debate. What may be new is the specific packaging: a release-objection argument for self-promising that depends on psychological discontinuity, plus the comparative claim that discontinuous agents can bind themselves where continuous agents cannot. That packaging faces serious problems a referee would press.

(1) Dilemma on identity. If the stages are discontinuous enough not to share a will, then on the Parfitian view you invoke this is just a promise to someone else, and nothing about self-promising has been vindicated. If they are the same self in the relevant sense, the release objection returns. The thesis trades on calling the relation 'self' while treating it as interpersonal.

(2) The release objection is synchronic. It says the person holding the claim can waive it at the time of performance. A continuous agent's earlier and later stages also do not exercise a single will at one time. So if temporal separation suffices, continuity is irrelevant and your comparative claim fails. If temporal separation does not suffice, you owe an account of why discontinuity, rather than mere non-simultaneity, does the work.

(3) Timing and capacity in the dementia case. Suppose performance is due from the pre-dementia stage while the promisee is the later stage. Then the promisee does not yet exist, or is not yet discontinuous, when performance is due. That raises the standard problems of promising to non-existent or not-yet-existent promisees: acceptance, uptake, standing. Separately, if the later stage lacks normative capacities, it cannot release, but it also plausibly cannot hold a claim in the full promissory sense. Binding then comes at the cost of the promise being owed to no competent promisee. Your sketch also leaves unclear which stage is obligated ('or vice versa'). The argument has to pick a direction, and each direction has a different problem.

(4) Exegesis. Check the Habib attribution. Cite Singer and the Kant paradox for the release objection. Note that Hobbes's dictum is about the sovereign and civil law.

Verdict: 'partly'. The paper would need to engage Schofield and Muñoz directly and show what discontinuity adds beyond temporal distinctness.

title: Content-Relative Continuity
thesis: What a promise requires of the performing stage is not global psychological continuity with the promising stage but continuity of the specific capacities and attitudes the promised performance draws on. Promissory binding is therefore relative to content.
argument_sketch: A promise to repay money can be kept by a stage with almost no psychological connection to the promiser, provided it controls the relevant funds. A promise to remain faithful to a lover requires continuity of the attitudes that constitute fidelity, and cannot be honored by a stage that lacks them, however continuous it is otherwise. Parfit's view that what matters is Relation R is too coarse, because it treats all psychological connections as equally relevant to all obligations. I argue that the promise's content determines which connections are relevant. This explains why a demented patient may still be bound by a financial commitment but not a relational one, why an AI instance may be bound to a factual task but not to an expressive commitment, and why corporate commitments survive turnover while those dependent on particular individuals do not.
why_new: Parfitian reductionism makes identity-relevant connections uniform across obligations. Identity-based views make identity all-or-nothing. This thesis introduces a third option, binding relative to the performance-relevant connections, which yields differentiated verdicts within each case type. Neither position in the existing literature captures that differentiation.

objection.objection: The argument conflates two different questions: who remains bound by a promise, and what it takes to fulfil it. Content plainly fixes the second. Repaying money requires control of funds; fidelity requires certain attitudes. But that tells us nothing about the first, which is the question Parfit's Relation R addresses. Once the two are separated, both anchor cases turn against the thesis. (1) The repayment case shows only that the performance is delegable. A guardian, an executor, or a stranger can discharge a debt, so the debt survives because nothing about the original promisor needs to survive. That is a fact about assignable or vicarious performance (cf. Hart on transferable rights; Raz on delegable duties), not evidence that a thin, content-specific continuity is what binds. (2) The fidelity case is a reductio. If a stage that lacks the attitudes constituting fidelity is not bound by the promise, then a spouse who falls out of love has been released rather than having broken the promise. The promise is defeated by exactly the failure it was meant to guard against. Promising exists precisely so that obligation persists when the motivating attitude lapses (Hume, Treatise 3.2.5; Scanlon's Principle F). The thesis therefore makes every attitude-dependent promise self-cancelling. What the examples actually support is weaker: inability to perform can excuse or defeat an obligation (ought-implies-can). Parfit can accept that without modification. So the thesis is either false (losing an attitude releases you) or trivial (inability excuses). Either way it is not a new account of promissory binding.
objection.rationale: This objection strikes the core inference, not a side claim. Both examples meant to establish content-relative binding are better explained by delegability and by ought-implies-can. The explanation the author offers yields a clearly unacceptable result: unfaithful promisors are released, not in breach. The extensions inherit the same flaw. The demented patient's financial obligation survives via guardianship and estate law, which supports the delegability reading. The AI and corporate cases likewise run on institutional succession, not psychological continuity. The treatment of Parfit compounds the problem. Reasons and Persons explicitly allows that commitments weaken with reduced connectedness (the Russian nobleman case; the discussion of degrees of connectedness in Part III), so the charge that R is 'too coarse' targets a position Parfit does not hold. A repair would require a principled distinction between lacking a capacity (which might release you) and failing to exercise it (which is breach), and then an argument that this distinction tracks continuity rather than mere ability. Without that, the thesis does not survive.

closest_work.work: David Shoemaker, 'Personal Identity and Practical Concerns', Mind 116 (2007); see also his SEP entry 'Personal Identity and Ethics'
closest_work.relation: Closest structural precedent. Shoemaker argues that different practical concerns (responsibility, compensation, self-concern, etc.) track different relations, so no single identity relation grounds them all. Your thesis applies this concern-pluralism within one concern, promissory obligation, indexed to promise content. That is a refinement of a published framework, not a new framework.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, 'Later Selves and Moral Principles' (1973, in Montefiore ed., Philosophy and Personal Relations); Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III, including the Russian nobleman case
closest_work.relation: Parfit already asks whether commitments bind weakly connected later selves, and treats connectedness as coming in degrees and kinds. He also allows that some connections (e.g., intention-fulfilment) may matter more than others. Your charge that R 'treats all psychological connections as equally relevant to all obligations' misdescribes him. The nobleman case is also the standard counterexample your view must answer.

closest_work.work: Contract-law doctrine on delegable vs. personal performance, e.g., Restatement (Second) of Contracts §§262, 318; the civilian notion of obligations intuitu personae
closest_work.relation: Law has long held that money debts survive death and incapacity (the estate pays) and are delegable, while personal-service obligations lapse when the particular person cannot perform. Your repayment/fidelity contrast and your corporate-turnover point reproduce this distinction almost exactly. The novelty would have to lie in a philosophical grounding the doctrine lacks, which the sketch does not yet supply.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Dworkin on Dementia', Hastings Center Report (1995); Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993); Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', Phil & Public Affairs (1999); Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (2002)
closest_work.relation: This is the established debate on whether earlier commitments bind or govern a demented later self, and on which capacities (valuing, interests, psychological unity) are relevant. Your dementia example lands in it without engaging it. Jaworska's capacity-specific account is especially close in spirit.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency (1998); Christian List and Philip Pettit, Group Agency (2011)
closest_work.relation: Both already explain how group agents' commitments persist through turnover of members, via the rational unity of the group agent. Your corporate case is covered there, and on grounds that do not obviously require content-relativity.

closest_work.work: Marya Schechtman, The Constitution of Selves (1996) and Staying Alive (2014); Hilde Lindemann, Holding and Letting Go (2014)
closest_work.relation: These offer relational and narrative accounts of how identity-dependent commitments (especially intimate ones) fare across dementia. They are directly relevant to your fidelity case.

novelty.note: The general idea is published: which psychological relations matter is relative to the practical concern (Shoemaker; implicitly Parfit). So is the doctrine that some obligations can be discharged by anyone controlling the relevant means while others are tied to the particular performer (contract law; group-agency literature). The AI-instance application may be newer, but that alone is a thin contribution. What could be novel is the specific claim that promissory *bindingness*, not merely the possibility of fulfilment, is relativized stage-by-stage to content. As sketched, the argument does not establish that claim, for four reasons. (1) It conflates being bound with being able to perform. That a stage lacking the attitudes of fidelity cannot honor the promise follows from ought-implies-can plus the promise's content. It shows nothing about identity or about what binding consists in. (2) The repayment case cuts the wrong way. If any stage controlling the funds can discharge the debt, that is because the obligation attaches to assets and transfers like a lien. It does not show that the debt binds a psychologically disconnected stage *as promisor*. (3) The view invites self-release. If a relational promise binds only stages that retain the constitutive attitudes, then a promisor can escape it by letting those attitudes lapse. But guarding against exactly that lapse is the point of such promises (Parfit's nobleman; Scanlon, What We Owe to Each Other, ch. 7, on the assurance interest). You must block this or bite the bullet. (4) 'Fidelity' needs disambiguation. On the dominant behavioral reading, a severely demented spouse can remain faithful, so the example does not support the thesis. On an attitudinal reading, you inherit the prior question, much discussed, of whether one can promise attitudes at all. Revise to (a) engage Shoemaker and the dementia literature directly, (b) correct the reading of Parfit, (c) separate bindingness from performability, and (d) answer the self-release objection. Without these, the paper is a restatement of known material.

title: Branching Promisors Owe Jointly, Not Severally
thesis: When a promising agent branches into multiple discontinuous successors, as when a conversational AI is instantiated in many parallel sessions or a corporation splits, the promise binds the branches jointly and not each branch severally. The obligation is collective and is discharged when any branch performs.
argument_sketch: Parfit's fission cases suggest that if identity is not what matters, both fission products inherit whatever matters, including obligations. But if each branch were severally bound, a single promise would multiply into many obligations, which is absurd: one promise to pay $100 cannot create a debt of $100 per instance. The resulting structure is that of joint obligation, familiar from law: each branch is answerable, but performance by one discharges all. I show that this structure follows from the promisee's interest, which is in one performance, not many. Collective-obligation theory (Collins, Björnsson) supplies the account of how unstructured groups can hold such duties. The view also yields distinctive verdicts about blame: no single branch is blameworthy for collective non-performance unless it could have performed.
why_new: Fission cases in personal-identity theory have been used to test theories of prudential concern, not of obligation. This thesis applies them to promissory obligation, identifies a multiplication problem the existing literature has missed, and resolves it with the joint/several distinction from law and collective-obligation theory.

objection.objection: The argument for jointness rests on a false dichotomy, and the structure it ends up endorsing is several liability, not joint liability. The reductio claims that several obligation would turn one $100 promise into n debts of $100. That holds only if each branch's duty has an agent-relative content: 'that I pay $100.' A promise's content is fixed by what was promised, which is that the promisee receives $100. Suppose each branch is severally bound to see to it that this one outcome obtains. Then there is one debt with n obligors, and one performance satisfies every branch's duty, because the single content is now fulfilled. This is exactly the liability the author borrows from law. 'Each branch is answerable, but performance by one discharges all' is the standard description of joint-and-several liability, and the 'several' half of that phrase is what makes each branch answerable. So the thesis's contrastive claim ('jointly and not severally') contradicts the structure the argument defends. The appeal to the promisee's interest in one performance cannot decide between the views, because both predict single satisfaction. Once the multiplication worry is gone, nothing drives us to a collective obligation-bearer. The distributive reading inherited from Parfitian fission (each successor bound to an outcome-directed duty) is simpler, and it fits Parfit's own suggestion that what matters is inherited by each product. The collective-obligation machinery then cuts against the author. Collins (2013, 'Collectives' Duties and Collectivization Duties'; 2019, Group Duties) denies that unstructured collections can bear duties at all. Such collections get only member-level duties to form a collective or to coordinate, and these presuppose that members can communicate. Discontinuous parallel instances are the paradigm case where they cannot. Björnsson's shared obligations are likewise distributive 'we-ought' claims, grounded in joint ability, that place obligations on each member. Neither theorist supplies an irreducible joint duty for these cases, so the cited theory delivers several obligations. Finally, the distinctive blame verdict is idle. In fission each successor typically inherits full capacity to perform, so 'no branch is blameworthy unless it could have performed' leaves every non-performing branch blameworthy, which is what the several view already predicts.
objection.rationale: This objection removes the paper's main argument, the multiplication reductio, and shows the defended structure to be several liability under another name. The thesis is left with no distinctive content beyond 'one performance discharges the promise,' which rival views share. It is not fatal (5) because a more modest paper could survive. Such a paper might argue that discontinuity creates a coordination problem that the distributive view handles badly: a branch cannot know whether another has paid, so outcome-directed several duties may either overdetermine performance or leave every branch excused. A jointness thesis could be rebuilt around that problem. But that would be a different argument, and it would have to confront Collins's claim that a coordination failure among non-communicating agents produces no group duty at all. As written, the core contrast does not survive.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III, esp. the fission cases and the discussion of commitments and desert under reduced psychological connectedness
closest_work.relation: Source of the premise that fission products inherit what matters. Parfit already raises whether commitments and promises survive weakened connectedness, though not the joint-versus-several question for multiple successors. The thesis starts from here and is not anticipated by it.

closest_work.work: David Shoemaker, 'Responsibility without Identity', Harvard Review of Philosophy 18 (2012); also Shoemaker, 'Personal Identity and Ethics', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
closest_work.relation: Argues that responsibility-relevant relations can hold without identity, including in fission. This is the nearest philosophical treatment of how backward-looking normative status distributes across branches. Your blame verdicts need to engage it directly.

closest_work.work: Sixth Council Directive 82/891/EEC on the division of public limited companies, Art. 12 (now Directive (EU) 2017/1132, Art. 146); US successor-liability doctrine
closest_work.relation: The corporate half of the thesis is settled positive law. When a company divides, the recipient companies are jointly and severally liable for the transferred obligations, and one performance discharges the debt. This is exactly the 'each answerable, one performance discharges all' structure you claim to derive. The novelty therefore cannot lie in the structure or in its corporate application.

closest_work.work: Stephanie Collins, Group Duties: Their Existence and Their Implications for Individuals (OUP, 2019)
closest_work.relation: Cited as support, but Collins denies that unstructured groups (her 'combinations' and 'coalitions') can bear duties. Only collectives with group-level decision procedures can. Parallel AI instances or newly split firms without a common decision procedure would therefore be, on her view, individuals each bearing their own duties. That is closer to the several reading you reject. You are citing her for the opposite of her view.

closest_work.work: Gunnar Björnsson, 'Essentially Shared Obligations', Midwest Studies in Philosophy 38 (2014)
closest_work.relation: A better fit for unstructured groups, but his account of shared obligation and members' blameworthiness gives a different blame verdict from yours. On his view, members can be blameworthy for failing to do their part in an achievable joint performance, even if no single member could have performed alone.

closest_work.work: David Chalmers, 'What We Talk to When We Talk to Language Models' (2025)
closest_work.relation: Discusses whether the interlocutor is the model, an instance, a thread, or a character, which is the identity question your AI case presupposes. It does not, to my knowledge, address promissory obligation across instances. Your application to AI is the most plausibly new contribution, and it needs to take a position on Chalmers's question first.

novelty.note:
I know of no paper defending exactly this thesis for promises across AI instances. I cannot rule one out in the recent AI-ethics literature, so search PhilPapers for 'promise' with 'fission', 'duplication', or 'instances' before claiming novelty. The thesis is still at most partly novel. The joint-and-several structure, and its application to splitting corporations, is black-letter law. The fission premise is Parfit's, and the inheritance of responsibility through fission is Shoemaker's territory. The argument also has substantive problems a referee would press.

(1) Terminology. What you describe (each branch answerable, one performance discharges all) is joint-and-several or solidary liability, not 'joint' obligation. Under strict joint liability, each party is liable only together with the others, or only for a share. You also slide between this legal structure and Collins/Björnsson-style collective obligation, where the duty-bearer is the group. These are different views with different implications, and the paper must pick one.

(2) The multiplication argument fails. Several obligations need not multiply performances. Suppose each branch is severally bound to see to it that the promisee receives $100 once. Then there are n obligations with one shared object, discharged by a single payment. That is the familiar structure of several duties with a common content, as when each of several lifeguards must ensure the swimmer is rescued. So the 'absurdity' does not favor collective over several bearers. It only rules out the uncharitable content 'each must pay $100'.

(3) The interest-based derivation is too quick. Many accounts deny that promissory obligation is grounded in the promisee's interest in performance. Owens (2012, Shaping the Normative Landscape) grounds it in an authority interest, and Shiffrin and Scanlon offer further alternatives. On authority views, the promisee may have a claim against each branch, which pushes toward severalty.

(4) The blame verdict is underspecified and possibly false. 'No branch is blameworthy unless it could have performed' ignores branches that could have coordinated, or could have enabled another branch to perform. The collective-responsibility literature you cite (and Feinberg 1968 before it) treats such members as blameworthy.

(5) The AI case needs an account of what the promising agent is. If the promisor is the model, or the thread rather than the instance, then parallel sessions may not be fission at all. In that case the Parfitian framing is idle.

To claim real originality, show what the AI case adds beyond the corporate-division case that the law already handles. Then fix the Collins citation and repair the multiplication argument.

title: Promissory Counterpart Contextualism
thesis: Which later stage is bound by a promise is fixed by a counterpart relation that is contextually selected by the reasonable understanding shared by promisor and promisee at the time of promising. There is no context-independent fact about whether a discontinuous stage is 'the same promisor'.
argument_sketch: On a stage-theoretic metaphysics (Sider, Lewis), what makes a later stage 'mine' is a counterpart relation, and counterpart relations are contextually variable. I argue that promising is a paradigm of a context that selects a counterpart relation. A user promising to 'remember this' to a conversational AI selects 'the same deployment' or 'the same model'. A family member promising a person with dementia selects 'the same organism under care'. A business partner selects 'the same legal entity'. The obligation then attaches to whichever later stage stands in that relation, whatever its psychological continuity. This explains why disagreements about these cases often feel like disagreements about what was really promised: they are disputes about which counterpart relation was salient. It also provides a non-arbitrary procedure for resolving them.
why_new: Counterpart theory has been applied to modality and to persistence but not to normative relations such as obligation. This thesis argues that promising is a context in which the counterpart relation is set interpersonally, so that the metaphysics of persistence is partly fixed by normative practice.

objection.objection: The account conflates the semantics of de re attributions with the normative grounds of obligation, and so it either overgenerates or quietly reinstates the context-independent fact it denies. Sider's (Four-Dimensionalism, 2001, ch. 5) and Lewis's ('Counterparts of Persons and Their Bodies', 1971) contextual flexibility concerns what makes sentences like 'I will be bound' true in a context. It does not concern what makes a later stage actually subject to a duty. Promissory obligation is generated by a normative power to bind oneself (Hart 1955; Raz 1977; Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape, 2012). Its scope is limited to the promisor, and that limit is not up for negotiation by the parties. If the parties' shared understanding is free to select any counterpart relation, the promisor can bind beings she has no authority over. Selecting 'same legal entity' binds future officers of the firm. Selecting 'same model' binds every other deployment, including ones serving other users. Selecting 'same family line' binds one's heirs. The parties could also select a gerrymandered relation ('stages that still endorse this promise') that makes the promise binding on no one, so the promisor escapes the obligation by construal. The paper's own examples show that the context does not merely reweight a similarity relation among stages of one object. It switches the object: the firm, the model weights, the organism. So the promise ends up binding a different entity than the one who exercised the power. To block these results, the author must restrict which counterpart relations a promising context may select. The only principled restriction is something like 'relations under which the later stage is the promisor in the sense required for self-binding authority.' That is a context-independent constraint on being the same promisor, which contradicts the thesis's second sentence. Dilemma: without the constraint, the view licenses binding third parties and evading by construal. With it, the view is false as stated, and the real work is done by a non-contextual criterion the paper never supplies.
objection.rationale: This attacks the central inference, not a peripheral example. The move from 'counterpart relations are contextually variable' to 'promising contexts fix who is bound' needs a bridge principle linking attribution-semantics to normative authority, and none is offered. The overgeneration cases are not exotic: the AI-deployment and legal-entity examples are the paper's own showcase cases, and they are exactly where the object switches. The claim to a 'non-arbitrary procedure' also collapses. The procedure is either unconstrained, and therefore arbitrary in just the way that matters (parties can stipulate burdens onto non-parties), or it is constrained by a criterion the thesis disavows. I rate it 4 rather than 5 because a repair is conceivable. The author could keep contextual selection but bound it by an independent account of self-binding authority, with context choosing only among relations that already satisfy that account. But that repair abandons the thesis's strong anti-realist second claim and demotes context to a tie-breaker within a space fixed by non-contextual facts. That is a substantially weaker and less novel paper. A secondary worry compounds the problem. The genuinely disputed cases (dementia, AI memory) are precisely those where there was no shared reasonable understanding at the time of promising. So even the constrained version gives the least guidance exactly where guidance is claimed.

closest_work.work: Theodore Sider, Four-Dimensionalism (OUP 2001), esp. ch. 5; also 'All the World's a Stage', AJP 74 (1996)
closest_work.relation: Supplies the core machinery. Temporal counterpart relations are context-dependent, and there is no context-independent answer to whether a discontinuous later stage is 'me' (Sider applies this to fission and puzzle cases). What your thesis adds is only the claim that a promising context selects the relation. So the metaphysical half is Sider's, not yours.

closest_work.work: Theodore Sider, 'Criteria of Personal Identity and the Limits of Conceptual Analysis', Philosophical Perspectives 15 (2001)
closest_work.relation: Argues that personal-identity talk is semantically indeterminate or context-relative and that practical contexts resolve it. This anticipates your claim that disputes over puzzle cases are disputes about which relation is salient.

closest_work.work: David Lewis, 'Counterparts of Persons and Their Bodies', JPhil 68 (1971); 'Survival and Identity' (1976)
closest_work.relation: The origin of inconstant counterpart relations: different contexts select personal versus bodily counterparts. Your 'same organism under care' versus 'same psychology' contrast is Lewis's person/body case with a normative application.

closest_work.work: David Braddon-Mitchell & Kristie Miller, 'How to Be a Conventional Person', The Monist 87 (2004); also Miller's later work on conventionalism about persistence
closest_work.relation: Develops the view that which stages count as the same person is fixed by contextually or communally operative conventions, with explicit attention to practical concerns. This is the closest competitor to your 'no context-independent fact' claim. You need to say what the promising context adds beyond a convention.

closest_work.work: Mark Johnston, 'Relativism and the Self' (in Krausz, ed., Relativism: Interpretation and Confrontation, 1989); cf. 'Human Beings', JPhil 1987
closest_work.relation: Johnston discusses (and largely resists) the idea that personal identity is fixed by our identity-related practices or conventions. It is an obvious objector for you to engage.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), the young Russian nobleman case and the discussion of promises and psychological discontinuity
closest_work.relation: The locus classicus for whether a commitment binds a psychologically discontinuous later self, and for treating the answer as partly a matter of how the parties conceive the commitment. Your project answers Parfit's question with Sider's tools.

closest_work.work: David Shoemaker, 'Personal Identity and Practical Concerns', Mind 116 (2007); Marya Schechtman, Staying Alive (2014)
closest_work.relation: Both argue that different practices (responsibility, care, prudence) track different relations, and Schechtman explicitly uses the dementia-care context. Your 'family member / organism under care' case is close to Schechtman's person-life view. Their pluralism lacks your counterpart semantics but reaches similar verdicts.

closest_work.work: Carol Rovane, The Bounds of Agency (1998)
closest_work.relation: Individuates persons by unified rational agency and commitments, including group persons. This is relevant to your legal-entity and AI-deployment cases, where the bearer of the commitment is not a human stage at all.

closest_work.work: David Chalmers, 'What We Talk To When We Talk To Language Models' (c. 2025, preprint; verify citation)
closest_work.relation: If I recall correctly, it asks whether the interlocutor is the model, an instance, a thread, or a character, and treats the answer as partly context-dependent. This closely parallels your 'same deployment vs same model' case and would need citing.

novelty.note:
I know of no paper arguing that the act of promising is itself what selects the temporal counterpart relation that fixes the obligation-bearer. In that narrow sense the thesis is novel. But each component is established: context-variable counterpart relations (Lewis, Sider); context- or convention-relative personal identity (Sider 2001b, Braddon-Mitchell & Miller); and different practices tracking different persistence relations (Shoemaker, Schechtman). The contribution is therefore an application. It will be judged on whether the application does work the existing views don't, and as sketched it has four problems.

(1) Idleness. A standard promise theory, whether Scanlon's fidelity principle or Owens' authority view, already fixes the content of the promise by the parties' reasonable shared understanding. 'I will remember this' as said by a deployment can simply be read as a promise that this deployment will retain it. Then the promisor's identity is not in question, only the content. You need a case where content-interpretation leaves the bearer undetermined and counterpart selection settles it. Otherwise Ockham cuts the metaphysics.

(2) Promisor and promisee are conflated. In the dementia case the person whose persistence is in doubt is the promisee, not the promisor. In the AI case as you phrase it ('a user promising... to a conversational AI'), it is again the promisee. Your thesis is about which later stage is bound. Those cases concern which later stage is owed. That is a different question, and it is the one Dworkin, Dresser and Jaworska debate under precedent autonomy.

(3) The business-partner case doesn't fit stage theory. The promisor is a legal entity. Its persistence is stipulated by law, not selected by a counterpart relation among a person's stages. Either broaden the thesis to non-person agents (and engage Rovane, and List & Pettit on group agency) or drop the case.

(4) 'Non-arbitrary procedure' is overclaimed. The hard cases are exactly those where the parties' understandings diverge or never reached the eventuality, such as a model update or unforeseen dementia. 'Reasonable shared understanding' then either makes the obligation indeterminate or smuggles in a default relation. Either way you face Sider's own admission that context sometimes fails to select. You owe an account of the default.

A stronger paper would concede the metaphysics to Sider and Braddon-Mitchell & Miller. It would locate novelty in a thesis about the normative structure of promising: that promissory uptake is a mechanism of counterpart selection with distinctive authority, unlike mere conversational salience. It would then confront the content-interpretation alternative in (1) directly.

title: Testamentary Commitments: No Self-Binding, Only Executors
thesis: An agent cannot bind a psychologically discontinuous future stage by promise. What appear to be such promises are testamentary acts, which bind no successor and instead impose duties on third parties (executors) to see the agent's intentions realized.
argument_sketch: A will does not bind the testator's successors. It binds executors to carry out the testator's instructions, within legal limits. The cases of advanced dementia, memoryless AI, and complete corporate turnover share the will's structure: the agent who made the commitment is unavailable at execution time. I argue that the power of self-binding (Raz, Owens) is a power over one's own normative situation, and a discontinuous future stage's situation is not one's own in the required sense. So self-binding is unavailable. The normative upshot of such commitments is real but redirected: carers, operators, and corporate officers incur duties to give effect to the original intentions. The view explains why we hold those third parties responsible and avoids the implausibility of blaming a demented patient or a fresh AI instance.
why_new: Discussions of posthumous harm (Feinberg, Pitcher) ask whether the dead can be wronged. This thesis reverses the question and asks whether a 'dead' (discontinuous) promisor can bind, then answers it using the structure of testamentary law. It is a principled skeptical position that still explains the residual normativity skeptics usually cannot.

objection.objection: The argument's own premise defeats its positive half. Self-binding is a power over one's own normative situation (Raz 1972, 'Voluntary Obligations and Normative Powers'; Owens 2012, Shaping the Normative Landscape). A discontinuous future stage's situation is not 'one's own' in the required sense, so the agent cannot bind it. But then a fortiori the agent cannot bind carers, operators, or corporate officers, whose normative situations are even more clearly not the agent's. The testamentary model only hides this. Executors are not bound by the testator's act. They are bound by their voluntary acceptance of the office and by the legal institution that defines it. A testator who names an executor who declines imposes no duty on anyone. So the 'real but redirected' upshot cannot flow from the agent's commitment. Either third-party duties have an independent ground (role acceptance, fiduciary law, professional or care obligations, duties of respect toward the person's past wishes), and the original act is normatively idle. Or the agent can impose duties on others by unilateral declaration, which is far stronger than the self-binding the paper denies. The corporate case sharpens this. With complete turnover of personnel, a bond covenant still binds the corporation, not its officers in their own right. The obligation tracks the institutional agent, not psychological continuity, and nothing about it is testamentary.
objection.rationale: The objection does not touch the negative thesis that discontinuous stages cannot be self-bound, though that thesis has its own problem: it assumes a psychological-continuity account of whose situation is 'one's own,' which begs the question against animalists (Olson 1997) and against defenders of precedent autonomy in dementia (Dworkin 1993; cf. Dresser 1986, Jaworska 1999). But the objection guts what makes the paper distinctive. The paper sells the testamentary reconstruction as preserving the normative force of such commitments and explaining why we hold third parties responsible. If that force comes from role acceptance, institutions, or independent duties of respect, the will analogy explains nothing, and the view collapses into an error theory: such 'promises' generate no obligation from the act itself. That is a defensible position but a much less interesting one. The view also loses its claimed advantage over rivals, since any view can say carers have role-based duties to honor prior wishes. The corporate case is plausibly a direct counterexample to the claim that the three cases share the will's structure. A fix is possible. The author could specify a mechanism by which the original act conditions or triggers duties that are independently grounded, such as Owens's interest in authority, or a Scanlonian expectation principle extended to those who take up a role. But that requires substantial new argument, not a clarification, so the objection rates a 4 rather than a 5.

closest_work.work: Allen Buchanan, 'Advance Directives and the Personal Identity Problem', Philosophy & Public Affairs 17 (1988); and Buchanan & Brock, Deciding for Others (1989)
closest_work.relation: Closest precedent for the dementia core. Buchanan takes up the 'someone else' problem: if the demented patient is not the author of the directive, what authority does the directive have? He grounds it in the surviving interests of the prior person, modeled on posthumous interests and testamentary disposition. That is your testamentary analogy, used to defend the directive's force. Your redirection to third-party duties is a short step from his position.

closest_work.work: Rebecca Dresser, 'Life, Death, and Incompetent Patients' (Arizona Law Review 1986); 'Dworkin on Dementia' (Hastings Center Report 1995); 'Bound to Treatment: The Ulysses Contract' (HCR 1984)
closest_work.relation: Holds that psychological discontinuity defeats the then-self's authority over the now-self. She explicitly rejects the will analogy because the 'estate' is a living patient with present interests. You need to answer this objection, and the sketch does not.

closest_work.work: Ronald Dworkin, Life's Dominion (1993), ch. 8 ('precedent autonomy')
closest_work.relation: The main opposing view. Advance directives bind through critical interests that persist into dementia. Your thesis is largely a denial of Dworkin's view, so it has to be positioned against him.

closest_work.work: Derek Parfit, Reasons and Persons (1984), Part III
closest_work.relation: Already argues that weakened psychological connectedness weakens the obligation to keep commitments made by earlier selves. It also suggests treating distant earlier and later selves more like other people. Your general metaphysical premise comes from here.

closest_work.work: Jennifer Radden, Divided Minds and Successive Selves (MIT, 1996)
closest_work.relation: Asks directly whether earlier 'successive selves' can bind later ones, with Ulysses contracts as the test case. She concludes that such binding is better understood as other-regarding. This is very close to your structural claim.

closest_work.work: Jon Elster, Ulysses and the Sirens (1979); Ulysses Unbound (2000)
closest_work.relation: Shows that much 'self-binding' actually works by placing duties or powers in third parties, as Ulysses does with his crew. Your claim that the commitment is redirected to executors repeats this structural point in the language of normative powers.

closest_work.work: Jeff McMahan, The Ethics of Killing (2002), ch. 5; David DeGrazia, Human Identity and Bioethics (2005), ch. 5; Agnieszka Jaworska, 'Respecting the Margins of Agency', PPA 28 (1999); Seana Shiffrin, 'Autonomy, Beneficence, and the Permanently Demented' (2004)
closest_work.relation: The standard literature on the authority of advance directives under weakened psychological unity. Each gives a worked-out account of which party bears which duty. You need to show why your view improves on theirs.

closest_work.work: Joseph Raz, 'Voluntary Obligations and Normative Powers' (PAS Supp. 1972) and 'Promises and Obligations' (1977); David Owens, Shaping the Normative Landscape (2012)
closest_work.relation: Sources for the normative-power framework you rely on. Neither draws your conclusion. Owens grounds promissory obligation in the promisee's authority interest, not in the promisor's power over 'his own' situation, so he is a poor ally for your key premise.

closest_work.work: Christian List & Philip Pettit, Group Agency (2011)
closest_work.relation: Argues that group agents persist through complete member turnover because their identity lies in decision procedures, not personnel. This directly contradicts your corporate case.

novelty.note:
The dementia version of the thesis and the testamentary analogy are well-trodden ground (Buchanan, Dresser, Parfit, Radden), and the 'redirect to third parties' structure is Elster's. Possibly new: (i) using Raz/Owens normative powers as the mechanism, (ii) the unified treatment of dementia, memoryless AI, and corporate turnover, and (iii) the categorical claim that self-binding is impossible rather than merely weakened. I know of no published work making this argument specifically for memoryless AI instances, though I cannot rule it out. As a referee I would press five problems.

(1) The key premise, that a discontinuous stage's normative situation is 'not one's own in the required sense', simply restates the conclusion. It needs an independent criterion of ownership.

(2) The will analogy fails at the point Dresser identified. Wills dispose of property to which no living rival has a claim. An 'advance directive as testament' disposes of the body and life of an existing patient with present interests. Your view therefore licenses one person to direct third parties to control another person, which is normatively worse than self-binding, not a gentler substitute.

(3) The corporate case is not discontinuity. Law and group-agency theory both treat the corporation as the same promisor (successor liability), so turnover of officers is not turnover of the agent.

(4) A memoryless AI instance with the same weights keeps character, values, and standing intentions. On Parfit's own criteria that may be more connected than advanced dementia. Episodic memory loss alone does not deliver your conclusion, so the case is underdescribed.

(5) The claimed explanatory gain is small. Standard views already avoid blaming the demented patient or the fresh instance through excuse or incapacity, while keeping the obligation in place. Carers' and officers' duties are usually explained by their own roles and fiduciary relations, not by a testamentary transfer.

A publishable version would need to give up the categorical impossibility claim, or defend the 'ownership' criterion head-on, and engage Buchanan and Radden explicitly.
